---
title: "Multilevel Network Meta-Regression III: Numerical Integration Theory"
---

## Introduction {#sec-qmc-intro}

Here is the practical problem this chapter solves, stated for a health researcher before any mathematics.
Picture an aggregate-data trial of a new plaque-psoriasis drug that publishes only summaries: the mean
patient age, the mean baseline severity score, and the proportion of patients who are biomarker-positive.
We want the average probability that a patient on this arm achieves a treatment response, so that the trial
can be entered into a network and the drug compared indirectly against its competitors. Because the
response probability is a nonlinear (logistic) function of a patient's covariates, that average is an
integral over the arm's covariate distribution; and if we compute the integral badly, the modeled response
rate is wrong, the odds ratio of this drug versus a comparator is wrong, and the reimbursement
recommendation a health technology assessment (HTA) agency issues on the strength of that odds ratio is
wrong. This chapter is the mathematics of computing that integral well. Its organizing idea, which we
announce now and prove at the end (@sec-qmc-pipeline), is that the covariate points at which we evaluate the
model are chosen once, deterministically, and reused unchanged at every step of the model fit. That single
decision, invisible in the statement of the integral, is exactly what separates the method used in practice
from a naive random simulation, and it is the reason the chapter builds toward deterministic
quasi-Monte Carlo rather than stopping at ordinary Monte Carlo.

Chapter 20 reduced the entire aggregate-data contribution of multilevel network meta-regression
(ML-NMR) to a single integral. For an aggregate-data (AgD) study $j$ reporting an arm $k$ with covariate
density $f_j$, the aggregate-level mean outcome is the response-scale average of the individual conditional
mean (@def-aggregate-model),
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{X}} g^{-1}\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_1+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}+\gamma_k,
$$ {#eq-qmc-aggregation}
and the aggregation theorem (@thm-aggregation) showed that the AgD likelihood is built from this one
quantity. The aggregation-bias theorem (@thm-aggregation-bias) explained why the integral cannot be
shortcut by plugging the covariate mean into $g^{-1}$: for a nonlinear link the average of $g^{-1}(\eta)$
is not $g^{-1}$ of the average. Two links escaped: the identity link, where @eq-qmc-aggregation collapses
to a function of the mean alone (@thm-identity-link-exact), and the log link with jointly Gaussian
covariates, where the moment generating function (@def-mgf) supplies a closed form (@thm-log-link-mgf).
The link that matters most for health technology assessment, the logit, escaped neither: @eq-qmc-aggregation
has no elementary closed form for any non-degenerate covariate distribution (@thm-logit-no-closed-form).
The discrete-outcome aggregate likelihoods of Chapter 21, the Poisson and Poisson-binomial constructions
(@thm-poisson-aggregate, @thm-poisson-binomial-pgf) and their approximations (@thm-le-cam-tv,
@thm-adjusted-binomial), all rest on the same integral through the success probabilities
$p_{ijk}=g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$. ML-NMR is therefore only as good as our ability to evaluate
@eq-qmc-aggregation numerically. This chapter builds that ability from the ground up and proves the error
guarantees that make it trustworthy.

Two features of the problem dictate the machinery. First, the dimension. The integral runs over
$\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ where $d$ is the number of covariates entered into the model,
typically three to ten. Deterministic product quadrature, which is essentially perfect in one dimension,
collapses under the curse of dimensionality: $k$ nodes per axis means $k^{d}$ nodes in total, and the cost
of a fixed accuracy grows exponentially in $d$ (@thm-quadrature-error, @cor-tensor-quadrature-curse).
Plain Monte Carlo (MC) integration escapes the curse with a dimension-free root-mean-square error of order
$N^{-1/2}$ (@thm-mc-rmse), but $N^{-1/2}$ is slow, and, more damagingly, the re-randomization it requires
injects noise into the likelihood and destroys the smooth Hamiltonian that gradient-based Markov chain
Monte Carlo needs (@def-hmc, @carpenter2017stan). Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) keeps a single deterministic
point set and replaces randomness by uniformity, achieving an error of order $(\log N)^{d}/N$, nearly
$1/N$, governed by the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (@thm-koksma-hlawka) and realized by low-discrepancy
sequences such as Sobol' points (@def-sobol-net). This is the integration rule used throughout ML-NMR.

Second, the input. We do not know $f_j$. An AgD study reports marginal summaries of each covariate, a
mean and sometimes a standard deviation or a proportion, but almost never the joint distribution. The
device that turns marginal information into a full joint law is the copula. Sklar's theorem
(@thm-sklar) separates any joint distribution into its marginals and a copula carrying the dependence;
the Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula) supplies a default dependence structure parameterized by a
correlation matrix borrowed from individual patient data (IPD) or expert judgment; and the probability
integral transform (@thm-inverse-cdf) maps uniform inputs onto whatever marginal distribution each
covariate is assumed to follow. Assembling these pieces gives the ML-NMR integration pipeline
(@thm-hypercube-integration): generate Sobol' points in the unit hypercube, push them through a Gaussian
copula and inverse-CDF margins to land at covariate vectors distributed as $f_j$, and average
$g^{-1}(\eta_{jk})$ over them. We close with a fully worked logit example whose every node, weight, and
running estimate the reader can reproduce by hand, and a two-covariate trace that exhibits the copula step
explicitly.

Throughout, $g$ is the link function (@def-link-function), $\eta_{jk}$ the linear predictor of the
individual model (@def-individual-model), and $\Phi,\phi$ the standard normal distribution and density
functions. We write $\mathrm{expit}(z)=g^{-1}(z)=e^{z}/(1+e^{z})$ for the inverse logit, also called the logistic
function; a health researcher meets it as the map that turns a log-odds back into a probability. The
covariate density and distribution functions of study $j$ are $f_j$ and $F_j$, with marginal distribution
functions $F_{j,1},\dots,F_{j,d}$ and covariate correlation matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$, all from
[Notation](/notation.qmd). This chapter corresponds to results H.12 to H.19 of the proof catalogue.

We fix one concrete scenario now and return to it at every transition, so that each abstract object
acquires a definite job. It is the running thread of the chapter.

::: {#exm-qmc-psoriasis}
## Running example: an aggregate psoriasis arm
An aggregate-data (AgD) trial arm of a psoriasis biologic reports three covariate summaries and nothing
about their joint distribution: mean age $45$ years (standard deviation $12$), mean baseline severity score
$18$ (standard deviation $6$), and proportion biomarker-positive $0.30$. So $d=3$ covariates enter the
model: $x_1=\text{age}$, $x_2=\text{baseline severity}$, $x_3=\text{biomarker status}$. From an
individual-patient-data (IPD) study in the same network we have fitted the individual model, a logistic
regression whose linear predictor $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$ combines a study baseline, prognostic effects, and
treatment-by-covariate interactions (the effect modifiers), and from that IPD study we also borrow a
covariate correlation matrix, say age and severity correlated at $0.3$. Our target is the arm's average
response probability
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{expit}\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$
the number that, contrasted with the same quantity on a comparator arm, becomes the odds ratio the HTA
agency will act on. Everything the chapter builds is in service of computing this one integral: the
**margins** ($x_1,x_2$ modeled as normal from the reported means and standard deviations, $x_3$ as a
Bernoulli from the reported proportion) fix each covariate's own distribution; the **copula** supplies the
missing dependence (which ages tend to accompany which severities); the **Sobol' nodes** are the covariate
profiles at which we evaluate $\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jk})$; and the **average** over those profiles is
$\theta_{\bullet jk}$. In @sec-qmc-example we carry a stripped-down version of this arm, a single
standardized severity covariate, all the way through the arithmetic to a final number a reader can check by
hand. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**What this chapter will do, in order.** The path from the integral to a trustworthy number has two halves,
a numerical half and a dependence-modeling half, and they meet in the pipeline of @sec-qmc-pipeline.

- Show why a covariate grid is hopeless beyond a few covariates (@sec-qmc-quadrature).
- Escape the curse with random Monte Carlo, then see why its noise is fatal inside a Bayesian fit
  (@sec-qmc-montecarlo).
- Replace random points with evenly spread deterministic ones and bound the error by the Koksma-Hlawka
  inequality (@sec-qmc-koksma), realized by Sobol' nets (@sec-qmc-sobol).
- Build synthetic covariate profiles from an AgD study's summaries using the probability integral transform
  (@sec-qmc-pit), Sklar's theorem (@sec-qmc-sklar), and the Gaussian copula (@sec-qmc-gaussian).
- Assemble the pipeline and prove its error bound (@sec-qmc-pipeline), then compute a full logit example by
  hand (@sec-qmc-example).

## Reducing the aggregation integral to the unit cube {#sec-qmc-reduction}

Every method in this chapter computes an integral against a probability density. It is convenient to fix,
once, the two equivalent forms in which @eq-qmc-aggregation will appear. The first is the
expectation form
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_j}\big[g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{X}))\big],
$$ {#eq-qmc-expectation}
which is what MC estimates directly by sampling $\mathbf{X}$. The second is the unit-cube form. Suppose we
have a map $T:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathcal{X}$ that transports the uniform distribution on the cube to $f_j$, in
the sense that $\mathbf{X}=T(\mathbf{U})$ has density $f_j$ whenever $\mathbf{U}$ is uniform on $[0,1]^{d}$.
In plain terms, $T$ is the recipe that turns a list of uniform numbers between $0$ and $1$ into a plausible
covariate profile for the aggregate study: feed it $(0.5,0.5,0.5)$ and it returns a patient of median age,
median severity, and so on; feed it a whole grid of uniform inputs and it returns a whole cloud of
synthetic patients whose distribution matches $f_j$. Constructing this recipe from the marginal and
correlation summaries an AgD study reports is the entire job of @sec-qmc-sklar to @sec-qmc-pipeline.

Then, writing $\varphi:=g^{-1}\circ\eta_{jk}$ for the integrand on covariate space and $\psi:=\varphi\circ T$
for its **pullback** to the cube (the same integrand, re-expressed as a function of the uniform inputs
$\mathbf{u}$ rather than of the covariates $\mathbf{x}=T(\mathbf{u})$), the change-of-variables identity
gives
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}
=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{U}\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{d})}\big[\psi(\mathbf{U})\big]
=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\psi(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u}.
$$ {#eq-qmc-pullback}

All @eq-qmc-pullback does is rename the variable of integration: the same average, first written over
covariate space with weight $f_j$, is rewritten over the unit cube with the flat (uniform) weight, at the
price of pushing the covariate values through the recipe $T$ inside the integrand. It is worth seeing a
first number before the machinery. Take the running example (@exm-qmc-psoriasis) stripped to a single
standardized severity covariate with a standard normal margin, so $T=\Phi^{-1}$ and, with a treatment arm
whose linear predictor is $\eta(x)=0.5+x$, the integrand on the cube is
$\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}\big(0.5+\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)$. Three evenly spread inputs already give a rough answer:

| $u$ | $x=\Phi^{-1}(u)$ | $\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}(0.5+x)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0.25$ | $-0.6745$ | $0.4565$ |
| $0.50$ | $0$ | $0.6225$ |
| $0.75$ | $0.6745$ | $0.7640$ |

Their average is $0.6143$, already within about $0.012$ of the true value $\theta_\bullet=0.6020$ that
@sec-qmc-example computes carefully. Everything between here and there is about choosing those input points
so that the average converges fast and smoothly, and about building $T$ for realistic multi-covariate arms.

The whole of the dependence-modeling apparatus, Sklar's theorem, the Gaussian copula, and the inverse-CDF
transform, exists to construct the transport map $T$ from the marginal and correlation summaries that an
AgD study reports; that construction is @sec-qmc-sklar to @sec-qmc-pipeline. The whole of the numerical
apparatus, quadrature, MC, and QMC, exists to approximate the cube integral on the right of
@eq-qmc-pullback by a finite average over points $\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}\subset[0,1]^{d}$,
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}\approx\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}g^{-1}\big(\eta_{jk}(T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)}))\big);
$$ {#eq-qmc-cubature}
that approximation, and its error, is @sec-qmc-quadrature to @sec-qmc-sobol. The single design decision
that ties the two halves together, and that distinguishes ML-NMR from a naive simulation, is that the
point set $\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}$ and the covariate nodes $\{T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})\}$ are fixed in advance and
reused at every evaluation of the likelihood; only $\eta_{jk}$, through the parameter vector
$\boldsymbol{\xi}$, changes as the sampler explores the posterior. We return to the consequences of that
decision in @sec-qmc-pipeline.

One notational caution before the numerical theory. The next three sections (@sec-qmc-quadrature to
@sec-qmc-koksma) are general facts about integrating a function over an interval or a cube, so they call
that function a generic $f$, in keeping with the numerical-analysis literature. This generic integrand $f$
is not the covariate density: our covariate density is $f_j$, and the specific integrand those theorems get
applied to is the ML-NMR pullback $\psi$ of @eq-qmc-pullback. When in doubt, $f$ inside a quadrature or
discrepancy theorem means "whatever function is being integrated," and for us that function is $\psi$.

## Gaussian quadrature and the curse of dimensionality {#sec-qmc-quadrature}

This section answers the first question a numerically minded reader asks: why not just lay down a grid of
covariate values, evaluate the model on the grid, and average? In one dimension a well-chosen grid is not
merely adequate, it is superb, and we prove exactly how superb. The catch is that the obvious way to build a
grid in several dimensions multiplies its size beyond reach, and that failure is what forces the rest of the
chapter. We begin with the gold standard for one-dimensional integration of a smooth function and then show
why it does not survive the passage to several covariates. The rule is Gauss-Legendre quadrature: choose $k$
nodes and $k$ weights, $2k$ numbers in all, and spend that budget so as to integrate exactly every
polynomial of degree up to $2k-1$. That maximal exactness is what gives Gauss quadrature its
super-algebraic accuracy on smooth integrands.

We prove the one-dimensional error formula in full, even though the curse of dimensionality will make us
abandon the method, because its error structure is the benchmark against which Monte Carlo and
quasi-Monte Carlo are measured for the rest of the chapter: it is the accuracy we are trading away in
exchange for freedom from the dimension. The proof uses two classical facts about the Legendre
polynomials $P_0,P_1,P_2,\dots$, the orthogonal polynomials on $[-1,1]$ (each $P_k$ has degree $k$, and
$\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)q(x)\,dx=0$ for every polynomial $q$ of degree below $k$; this orthogonality is the one
property we use). The second tool is Hermite interpolation: given $k$ nodes, the unique polynomial of
degree at most $2k-1$ that matches both $f$ and its derivative $f'$ at every node, whose remainder we quote
in the proof. Both are standard (Stoer and Bulirsch, Section 3.6, cited in @sec-qmc-notes); a reader
willing to take the error formula @eq-qmc-gauss-error on faith can skip the proof and lose nothing needed
later.

::: {#thm-quadrature-error}
## Gauss-Legendre quadrature error
Let $f\in C^{2k}[-1,1]$, that is, $f$ has $2k$ continuous derivatives on $[-1,1]$. Let $x_1,\dots,x_k$ be
the $k$ roots of the Legendre polynomial $P_k$ (orthogonal on $[-1,1]$ with respect to Lebesgue measure),
and let $w_1,\dots,w_k>0$ be the unique weights for which the rule
$$
Q_k[f]:=\sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i\,f(x_i)
$$
is exact on polynomials of degree at most $k-1$. Then:

1. **(Degree of exactness.)** $Q_k[p]=\int_{-1}^{1}p(x)\,dx$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most
$2k-1$.

2. **(Error formula.)** There exists $\xi\in(-1,1)$ such that
$$
\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx-Q_k[f]
=\frac{2^{2k+1}\,(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)\,[(2k)!]^{3}}\;f^{(2k)}(\xi).
$$ {#eq-qmc-gauss-error}

3. **(Composite order.)** If $[-1,1]$ is partitioned into panels of width $h$ and the $k$-node rule is
applied on each panel, the total error is $O(h^{2k})$ as $h\to 0$ with $k$ fixed and $f^{(2k)}$ bounded.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* The defining property of the Legendre polynomial $P_k$ is orthogonality:
$\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)q(x)\,dx=0$ for every polynomial $q$ with $\deg q<k$ (a classical fact about orthogonal
polynomials; see the references). Let $p$ have $\deg p\le 2k-1$. Polynomial division by $P_k$ writes
$p=q\,P_k+r$ with $\deg q\le k-1$ and $\deg r\le k-1$. Integrating,
$$
\int_{-1}^{1}p=\int_{-1}^{1}q\,P_k+\int_{-1}^{1}r=0+\int_{-1}^{1}r,
$$
the first integral vanishing by orthogonality since $\deg q<k$. Evaluating the rule, and using
$P_k(x_i)=0$ at every node,
$$
Q_k[p]=\sum_i w_i\big(q(x_i)P_k(x_i)+r(x_i)\big)=\sum_i w_i\,r(x_i)=Q_k[r].
$$
Because $\deg r\le k-1$, the rule integrates $r$ exactly by its defining property, so
$Q_k[r]=\int_{-1}^{1}r$. Combining, $Q_k[p]=\int_{-1}^{1}r=\int_{-1}^{1}p$.

*Part 2.* Let $H$ be the Hermite interpolating polynomial of degree at most $2k-1$ that matches $f$ and
$f'$ at each node: $H(x_i)=f(x_i)$ and $H'(x_i)=f'(x_i)$ for $i=1,\dots,k$. The Hermite remainder formula
states that for each $x\in[-1,1]$ there is $\zeta_x\in(-1,1)$ with
$$
f(x)-H(x)=\frac{f^{(2k)}(\zeta_x)}{(2k)!}\,\omega(x)^{2},
\qquad \omega(x):=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(x-x_i).
$$
Since $\deg H\le 2k-1$, Part 1 gives $Q_k[H]=\int_{-1}^{1}H$, and since $H(x_i)=f(x_i)$ we have
$Q_k[H]=Q_k[f]$. Therefore
$$
\int_{-1}^{1}f-Q_k[f]=\int_{-1}^{1}(f-H)
=\frac{1}{(2k)!}\int_{-1}^{1}f^{(2k)}(\zeta_x)\,\omega(x)^{2}\,dx.
$$
The kernel $\omega(x)^{2}\ge 0$, so the integral mean value theorem yields a single $\xi\in(-1,1)$ with
$$
\int_{-1}^{1}f-Q_k[f]=\frac{f^{(2k)}(\xi)}{(2k)!}\int_{-1}^{1}\omega(x)^{2}\,dx.
$$
It remains to evaluate $\int_{-1}^{1}\omega^{2}$. The nodes are the roots of $P_k$, so $\omega$ is the
monic Legendre polynomial: $\omega=P_k/c_k$, where $c_k=\dfrac{(2k)!}{2^{k}(k!)^{2}}$ is the leading
coefficient of the standard Legendre polynomial. With the normalization
$\int_{-1}^{1}P_k(x)^{2}\,dx=\dfrac{2}{2k+1}$,
$$
\int_{-1}^{1}\omega(x)^{2}\,dx=\frac{1}{c_k^{2}}\int_{-1}^{1}P_k^{2}
=\frac{2^{2k}(k!)^{4}}{[(2k)!]^{2}}\cdot\frac{2}{2k+1}
=\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{2}}.
$$
Dividing by $(2k)!$ gives the constant in @eq-qmc-gauss-error.

*Part 3.* On a panel $[a,a+h]$ substitute $x=a+\tfrac{h}{2}(1+t)$, so
$\int_a^{a+h}f=\tfrac{h}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}\tilde f(t)\,dt$ with $\tilde f(t)=f(a+\tfrac{h}{2}(1+t))$ and
$\tilde f^{(2k)}=(h/2)^{2k}f^{(2k)}$. Applying Part 2 to $\tilde f$, the panel error is
$$
\frac{h}{2}\cdot\frac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}\Big(\tfrac{h}{2}\Big)^{2k}f^{(2k)}(\xi_a)
=C_k\,h^{2k+1}f^{(2k)}(\xi_a),
$$
with $C_k=\dfrac{(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}$ a constant depending only on $k$. Summing over the $2/h$
panels and bounding $|f^{(2k)}|$ by its supremum,
$$
\Big|\int_{-1}^{1}f-\sum_{\text{panels}}Q_k\Big|
\le \frac{2}{h}\cdot C_k\,h^{2k+1}\sup_{[-1,1]}|f^{(2k)}|
=2\,C_k\,h^{2k}\sup_{[-1,1]}|f^{(2k)}|=O(h^{2k}).\qquad\square
$$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What "order $2k$" buys, and what it cannot.** The single-interval constant @eq-qmc-gauss-error decays
super-exponentially in $k$: by Stirling's approximation
$\dfrac{2^{2k+1}(k!)^{4}}{(2k+1)[(2k)!]^{3}}\sim\dfrac{\pi}{4^{k}\,(2k)!}$ (for $k=1$ the exact value is
$\tfrac13$), so for an analytic integrand whose derivatives satisfy $|f^{(2k)}|\le (2k)!\,R^{-2k}$ (radius
of convergence $R>1$) the error falls like $(2R)^{-2k}$, geometric in the number of nodes. This is the spectral accuracy that
makes a handful of Gauss nodes integrate a smooth one-dimensional function to machine precision. The
composite reading of Part 3, error $O(h^{2k})$ at fixed $k$, is the form quoted in the catalogue; it is the
relevant one when the integrand has limited smoothness and one refines the mesh rather than raising the
node count. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The trouble is that ML-NMR integrates over several covariates at once, and the only elementary way to lift
a one-dimensional rule to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is to take a tensor product: place a grid of $k^{d}$ nodes, one
factor per axis. The accuracy per axis is inherited, but the node count is not.

::: {#cor-tensor-quadrature-curse}
## The curse of dimensionality for product quadrature
Let $f\in C^{2k}([-1,1]^{d})$ with all pure $2k$-th order partial derivatives bounded. Split each axis
into $m$ panels of width $h=2/m$ and take the tensor product of the composite $k$-node Gauss-Legendre rules
of @thm-quadrature-error(3). This rule uses $N=(mk)^{d}$ function evaluations and, as $m\to\infty$ with $k$
fixed, has error
$$
\Big|\int_{[-1,1]^{d}} f-Q^{\otimes d}[f]\Big|=O\!\big(h^{2k}\big)=O\!\big(N^{-2k/d}\big).
$$
The exponent $2k/d$ of $N$ degrades with the dimension $d$; equivalently, to hold the error at a tolerance
$\epsilon$ the cost $N$ grows exponentially in $d$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $I_i$ for integration and $Q_i$ for the composite rule in coordinate $i$, so the error is
$I_1\cdots I_d f-Q_1\cdots Q_d f=\sum_{i=1}^{d}Q_1\cdots Q_{i-1}(I_i-Q_i)I_{i+1}\cdots I_d f$ (a telescoping
sum). In the $i$-th term, @thm-quadrature-error(3) bounds $|(I_i-Q_i)g|$ by $2C_kh^{2k}\sup|\partial_i^{2k}f|$
for every slice $g$ of $f$ in coordinate $i$; the remaining integrals have length $2$ per axis, and the
remaining rules have positive weights summing to $2$ per axis, so each term is at most
$2^{d-1}\cdot 2C_kh^{2k}\sup|\partial_i^{2k}f|$. Summing over $i$ gives error $O(h^{2k})$, and since
$N=(mk)^{d}=(2k/h)^{d}$ we have $h=2kN^{-1/d}$, so the error is $O(N^{-2k/d})$. $\square$
:::

The exponent $2k/d$ tells the whole story, and it is worth reading carefully because it is easy to
misread. With $k$ held fixed, refining a product grid improves the error only like $N^{-2k/d}$; and raising $k$ to
sharpen the per-axis accuracy multiplies the node count by $k^{d}$. In one dimension a composite five-node
rule ($k=5$) integrates a smooth function with error $O(N^{-10})$, spectacular; in ten dimensions the same
per-axis rule needs $N=5^{10}\approx 10^{7}$ nodes just to place five points on each axis, and its error
improves only like $N^{-1}$. To make the
threshold concrete, return to the running example (@exm-qmc-psoriasis). Three covariates at five nodes each
is $5^{3}=125$ nodes, which sounds harmless. But this integral is not evaluated once. It is evaluated once
per AgD arm; a plaque-psoriasis network may carry a dozen AgD arms; and the whole set of integrals is
recomputed at every leapfrog step of every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo fit, tens of thousands
of times. At $d=3$ the $125$-node grid is tolerable, but real ML-NMR analyses reach into more covariates:
in a plaque-psoriasis network the effect modifiers may include age, baseline severity, disease duration,
weight, and biomarker status; in a network of newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) treatments they may
include age, disease stage, and cytogenetic risk. At $d=8$, five nodes per axis is $5^{8}\approx 3.9\times
10^{5}$ nodes, multiplied again by arms and by tens of thousands of posterior evaluations: product
quadrature is out. ML-NMR routinely runs at $d=3$ to $10$, and the next two sections develop the two ways
around the curse, both of which decouple the error rate from $d$ in the exponent.

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters for indirect comparison.** Everything downstream of ML-NMR depends on
$\theta_{\bullet jk}$ being right. It is the modeled event rate on an AgD arm; the contrast of two such
rates on the linear-predictor scale is the relative effect that the network synthesizes, and it is the
number an HTA agency reads as the odds ratio of one drug versus another. A biased integral biases that odds
ratio and can flip a cost-effectiveness verdict. Product quadrature would in principle deliver the integral
to near-machine precision, but at the dimensions and repetition counts of a real network it is
computationally impossible, which is exactly why the reliable-but-slow and reliable-but-fast alternatives of
the following sections are needed rather than merely nice to have. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Monte Carlo integration and its dimension-free rate {#sec-qmc-montecarlo}

Monte Carlo integration replaces the deterministic grid by independent random draws. The plain-language
idea is one every health researcher already trusts: to estimate an average over a population, draw a random
sample and average over the sample. Here the "population" is the arm's covariate distribution $f_j$ and the
quantity averaged is the response probability $\mathrm{expit}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$, so we simulate many
synthetic patients from $f_j$, compute each one's modeled response probability, and average. The larger the
sample, the closer the sample average sits to the true integral; the price is that a random sample is
noisy, and halving that noise takes four times the sample. Its error analysis is nothing more than the
variance of a sample mean, but the conclusion is striking: the rate of convergence does not depend on the
dimension at all.

::: {#thm-mc-rmse}
## Monte Carlo root-mean-square error
Let $\mathbf{U}_1,\dots,\mathbf{U}_N$ be independent and identically distributed with common density $f$ on
a domain $\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$, let $h:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
$\sigma^{2}:=\mathrm{Var}_f(h(\mathbf{U}))<\infty$, and let $I=\mathbb{E}_f[h(\mathbf{U})]=\int_{\mathcal{D}}h\,f$.
The Monte Carlo estimator $\widehat I_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}h(\mathbf{U}_n)$ satisfies:

1. **(Unbiasedness.)** $\mathbb{E}[\widehat I_N]=I$.

2. **(Root-mean-square error.)** $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat I_N)=\sigma^{2}/N$, hence the root-mean-square error is
$$
\mathrm{RMSE}(\widehat I_N)=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\big[(\widehat I_N-I)^{2}\big]}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt N}=O(N^{-1/2}),
$$ {#eq-qmc-mc-rmse}
a rate that does not depend on the dimension $d$.

3. **(Asymptotic normality.)** $\sqrt N\,(\widehat I_N-I)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Each summand $h(\mathbf{U}_n)$ has, by construction, mean $I$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$.

*Part 1.* By linearity of expectation,
$\mathbb{E}[\widehat I_N]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[h(\mathbf{U}_n)]=\frac{1}{N}\cdot N I=I$.

*Part 2.* The draws are independent, so the covariances between distinct summands vanish and the variance
of the sum is the sum of the variances:
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\widehat I_N)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{Var}\big(h(\mathbf{U}_n)\big)
=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\cdot N\sigma^{2}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N}.
$$
Because $\widehat I_N$ is unbiased, its mean-square error equals its variance, and the root-mean-square
error is its square root, $\sigma/\sqrt N$. The variance
$\sigma^{2}=\int_{\mathcal{D}}\big(h(\mathbf{u})-I\big)^{2}f(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u}$ is a single number
attached to the integrand and the sampling law; the dimension $d$ enters only through that number, never
through the exponent of $N$.

*Part 3.* The variables $h(\mathbf{U}_n)$ are independent and identically distributed with finite variance
$\sigma^{2}$, so the Lindeberg-Lévy central limit theorem (the independent-and-identically-distributed
central limit theorem proved in Chapter 5) gives
$\sqrt N\,(\widehat I_N-I)=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(h(\mathbf{U}_n)-I\big)\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A free variance bound for bounded links.** For the logit link the integrand of @eq-qmc-pullback is
$\psi=\mathrm{expit}\circ\eta_{jk}\circ T\in(0,1)$. A random variable supported in $[0,1]$ has variance at
most $1/4$ (Popoviciu's inequality: the variance of a $[a,b]$-valued variable is at most $(b-a)^2/4$,
attained by the two-point law at the endpoints). Hence $\sigma^{2}\le 1/4$ and, for the logit aggregate
mean, the Monte Carlo root-mean-square error obeys the explicit, distribution-free bound
$\mathrm{RMSE}\le 1/(2\sqrt N)$ regardless of the covariate dimension. With $N=10^{4}$ draws this is at
most $0.005$ on the probability scale. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why ML-NMR does not use plain Monte Carlo.** Two defects rule it out as the integration rule inside a
Bayesian fit. The first is the rate: $N^{-1/2}$ is slow, and the integral in @eq-qmc-aggregation is
re-evaluated once per study and arm at every leapfrog step of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (@def-hmc), so a slow
rule multiplies the cost of the entire posterior computation. The second, and decisive, defect is
stochasticity. If the points $\mathbf{U}_n$ are redrawn at each likelihood evaluation, then
$\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ is a random function of the parameters, its gradient
in $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is corrupted by Monte Carlo noise, and the Hamiltonian that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
integrates is no longer conserved; the sampler's acceptance probability degrades and its stationarity
guarantee (@thm-mh-stationarity) is lost. Fixing a single point set removes the noise but forfeits the
independence on which @thm-mc-rmse rests. The resolution, deterministic low-discrepancy points, is the
subject of the next section. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**In plain terms: why a jittery likelihood breaks the fit.** The Bayesian fit that ML-NMR runs (Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo, @def-hmc, Chapter 24) explores the space of parameter values by rolling a ball across the
likelihood surface, using the slope (the gradient) of that surface to decide where to go next. This works
only if the surface is a fixed, smooth landscape: the same parameters must always give the same likelihood,
and nearby parameters must give nearby likelihoods. If we recompute the aggregation integral with a fresh
random sample of synthetic patients at each step, the surface trembles underfoot, the same parameters give a
slightly different height each time, the slope is corrupted by that trembling, and the ball wanders instead
of settling into the posterior. The cure is to fix the synthetic patients once, so the surface stands
still. That makes the likelihood reproducible and differentiable, at the cost of giving up the independence
that the Monte Carlo error bound relied on, which is why we need a new, deterministic error theory. The
three natural point-set choices line up as follows.

| Point-set choice | Error rate | Reproducible? | Smooth in the parameters? | Verdict for ML-NMR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fresh random points, redrawn each step | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | no | no (jitters) | breaks the fit |
| Fixed pseudorandom points, drawn once | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | yes | yes | usable but slow |
| Fixed Sobol' (low-discrepancy) points | $O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ | yes | yes | the method used |

Fixing the points already buys reproducibility and smoothness; choosing them to be evenly spread rather than
random buys, in addition, the far faster error rate. The next section proves that faster rate.
:::

## Quasi-Monte Carlo: the Koksma-Hlawka inequality {#sec-qmc-koksma}

Monte Carlo gave a probabilistic error, a variance that shrinks on average but leaves the realized error on
any one sample random. Having decided to fix the points once, we can no longer appeal to that probabilistic
argument, and we instead want a deterministic ceiling: a bound that holds for certain on the specific point
set we chose. Quasi-Monte Carlo keeps the equal-weight average of @eq-qmc-cubature but replaces the random
points by a deterministic set chosen to fill the cube as evenly as possible. The deterministic ceiling
factors, beautifully, into two independent pieces: how evenly the points are spread, and how wildly the
integrand moves. "Evenly spread" is made precise by **discrepancy**, a measure of how far the empirical
distribution of the points departs from the uniform distribution; "how wildly the integrand moves" is made
precise by its **variation**. The error is at most the product of the two: spread the points evenly (small
discrepancy) and the average is accurate unless the integrand is very rough (large variation). This clean
statement is the Koksma-Hlawka inequality. We first define its two ingredients, and after each definition
pause to say, in plain terms, what it measures.

::: {#def-star-discrepancy}
## Star discrepancy
For a point set $P_N=\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_N\}\subset[0,1]^{d}$ and a corner box
$[\mathbf{0},\mathbf{u})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[0,u_i)$, the **local discrepancy** is the signed gap between the
fraction of points in the box and its volume,
$$
\Delta_N(\mathbf{u})=\frac{1}{N}\,\#\{n:\mathbf{u}_n\in[\mathbf{0},\mathbf{u})\}-\prod_{i=1}^{d}u_i,
$$
and the **star discrepancy** is its worst case over all corner boxes,
$$
D_N^{*}(P_N)=\sup_{\mathbf{u}\in[0,1]^{d}}\big|\Delta_N(\mathbf{u})\big|.
$$ {#eq-qmc-star-disc}
A point set is said to be of **low discrepancy** if $D_N^{*}(P_N)=O\big((\log N)^{d}/N\big)$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: discrepancy is unevenness.** Discrepancy asks a simple fairness question. Take any
box anchored at the origin corner, say the lower-left quarter of the unit square; the fraction of your
points that fall inside it should be about its area, one quarter. Local discrepancy is the gap between the
actual fraction and the area for one such box, and star discrepancy is the worst gap over every anchored box
at once. A point set with small star discrepancy is evenly spread at every scale, with no clumps and no
gaps; a set with large star discrepancy has some region that is over- or under-populated. Independent random
points clump by chance and have star discrepancy of order $N^{-1/2}$; a low-discrepancy set drives it down
to nearly $1/N$, which is the whole source of the quasi-Monte Carlo advantage. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-hardy-krause-variation}
## Hardy-Krause variation
For $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ the **total variation** is
$V(f)=\sup\sum_{m}\big|f(t_{m})-f(t_{m-1})\big|$, the supremum over all partitions
$0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_M=1$; $f$ has **bounded variation** if $V(f)<\infty$, and then for $f\in C^{1}$,
$V(f)=\int_0^1|f'(t)|\,dt$. In $d$ dimensions, the **Vitali variation** $V^{(d)}(f)$ is the supremum over
grid partitions of $\sum|\Delta f|$, where $\Delta f$ is the $d$-fold alternating difference of $f$ over a
grid box; for $f\in C^{d}$, $V^{(d)}(f)=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\big|\partial_{1}\cdots\partial_{d}f\big|\,d\mathbf{u}$.
The **Hardy-Krause variation** anchored at $\mathbf{1}$ sums the Vitali variations of $f$ restricted to
every face of the cube,
$$
V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)=\sum_{\emptyset\ne J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}}V^{(|J|)}\big(f|_{J}\big),
$$ {#eq-qmc-hk}
where $f|_{J}$ is the restriction of $f$ to the face $\{u_i=1:i\notin J\}$, a function of the coordinates
indexed by $J$. $f$ has **bounded Hardy-Krause variation** if $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)<\infty$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: variation is total roughness.** This is the hardest definition in the chapter, so
here is the picture. In one dimension, total variation $V(f)$ is the total up-and-down travel of the graph:
add up every rise and every fall, and for a smooth $f$ this is $\int_0^1|f'|$. A gently sloping function has
small variation; a function that oscillates violently, or jumps, has large variation. The multivariable
generalization adds one new idea, the **alternating difference**, which measures not just up-and-down travel
but twisting. Over a rectangle $[a_1,b_1]\times[a_2,b_2]$ the two-dimensional alternating difference is the
signed corner sum
$$
f(b_1,b_2)-f(a_1,b_2)-f(b_1,a_2)+f(a_1,a_2),
$$
which is zero for any function that is additive in its two coordinates and grows only when the coordinates
interact; the Vitali variation $V^{(d)}$ totals the absolute alternating differences over all grid
rectangles, capturing how much the function twists across the interior. The Hardy-Krause variation then
totals the roughness over the whole cube and over every lower-dimensional face of it: for $d=2$ it sums the
ordinary variation of $f$ along the top edge ($J=\{1\}$), the ordinary variation along the right edge
($J=\{2\}$), and the Vitali variation over the whole square ($J=\{1,2\}$). The faces are taken at the top
corner, "anchored at $\mathbf{1}$": the coordinates not in $J$ are frozen at $1$, a bookkeeping convention
(one could equally anchor at $\mathbf{0}$) that ensures every face and the interior are counted once. The
one thing to remember is the headline: **$V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)$ is a single number, large when $f$ is rough,
jumpy, or strongly interacting, and small when $f$ is smooth and mild.** It is the $V_{\mathrm{HK}}$ of
[Notation](/notation.qmd), and in the error bound it plays exactly the role its name suggests: a penalty for
integrand roughness. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

In one dimension the face sum @eq-qmc-hk has the single term $J=\{1\}$, so $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)=V(f)$ is
ordinary total variation, and the corner boxes of @eq-qmc-star-disc are the intervals $[0,u)$. We prove
the inequality in full in this one-dimensional case, where it is due to Koksma, and then state the
multidimensional form due to Hlawka.

::: {#thm-koksma-hlawka}
## Koksma-Hlawka inequality
Let $f:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ have bounded Hardy-Krause variation $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)<\infty$. For every
point set $P_N=\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_N\}\subset[0,1]^{d}$,
$$
\bigg|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{u}_n)-\int_{[0,1]^{d}}f(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u}\bigg|
\;\le\; V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\,D_N^{*}(P_N).
$$ {#eq-qmc-kh}
Consequently, for a low-discrepancy point set the quasi-Monte Carlo error is
$O\big(V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\,(\log N)^{d}/N\big)$, nearly $1/N$ and, for moderate $d$, far better than the
$N^{-1/2}$ of plain Monte Carlo (@thm-mc-rmse).
:::

::: {.proof}
*The one-dimensional case ($d=1$), in full.* Take $f\in C^{1}[0,1]$; the general bounded-variation case is
recovered at the end. Let $P_N=\{u_1,\dots,u_N\}\subset(0,1)$, and let
$F_N(u)=\frac{1}{N}\#\{n:u_n\le u\}$ be the empirical distribution function of the points, a nondecreasing
step function rising from $0$ to $1$. The local discrepancy is $\Delta_N(u)=F_N(u)-u$, and by
@eq-qmc-star-disc, $D_N^{*}=\sup_{u\in[0,1]}|\Delta_N(u)|$.

Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to write each value as an integral of the derivative. For each
point, $f(u_n)=f(1)-\int_{u_n}^{1}f'(u)\,du=f(1)-\int_0^1\mathbf{1}\{u>u_n\}f'(u)\,du$. Averaging over $n$
and interchanging the finite sum with the integral,
$$
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(u_n)
=f(1)-\int_0^1\Big(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{u>u_n\}\Big)f'(u)\,du
=f(1)-\int_0^1 F_N(u)\,f'(u)\,du,
$$
where we used $\frac{1}{N}\sum_n\mathbf{1}\{u>u_n\}=F_N(u)$ for all but the finitely many $u\in P_N$, a set
of Lebesgue measure zero that does not affect the integral. The exact integral admits the same treatment:
substituting $f(u)=f(1)-\int_u^1 f'(t)\,dt$ and applying Fubini's theorem to swap the order of integration
over the triangle $\{0\le u\le t\le 1\}$,
$$
\int_0^1 f(u)\,du=f(1)-\int_0^1\!\!\int_u^1 f'(t)\,dt\,du
=f(1)-\int_0^1 f'(t)\Big(\int_0^t du\Big)dt=f(1)-\int_0^1 t\,f'(t)\,dt.
$$
Subtracting the two displays, the constants $f(1)$ cancel and the derivative integrals combine:
$$
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(u_n)-\int_0^1 f(u)\,du
=-\int_0^1\big(F_N(u)-u\big)f'(u)\,du=-\int_0^1\Delta_N(u)\,f'(u)\,du.
$$ {#eq-qmc-koksma-identity}
This is the one-dimensional Hardy-Krause identity: the integration error is the integral of the local
discrepancy against $df$. Bounding the integral by the supremum of $|\Delta_N|$ times the $L^1$ norm of
$f'$,
$$
\bigg|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(u_n)-\int_0^1 f\bigg|
\le\Big(\sup_{u\in[0,1]}|\Delta_N(u)|\Big)\int_0^1|f'(u)|\,du
=D_N^{*}\,V(f),
$$
using $V(f)=\int_0^1|f'|$ for $f\in C^1$ (@def-hardy-krause-variation). This is @eq-qmc-kh for $d=1$.

For general $f$ of bounded variation on $[0,1]$, replace the derivative integrals by Riemann-Stieltjes
integrals against $df$: integration by parts for the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, valid because the step
function $\Delta_N$ and the bounded-variation $f$ may be taken to share no discontinuities (perturb the
endpoints if necessary), gives
$\frac1N\sum_n f(u_n)-\int_0^1 f=\int_0^1 f\,d\Delta_N=-\int_0^1\Delta_N\,df$, and
$|\!\int_0^1\Delta_N\,df|\le\sup|\Delta_N|\int_0^1|df|=D_N^{*}V(f)$, where $\int_0^1|df|=V(f)$ is the total
variation. The bound @eq-qmc-kh follows in the same form.

*The multidimensional case.* The identity @eq-qmc-koksma-identity generalizes to
$$
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{u}_n)-\int_{[0,1]^{d}}f
=\sum_{\emptyset\ne J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}}(-1)^{|J|}\int_{[0,1]^{|J|}}
\Delta_N\big(\mathbf{u}_J,\mathbf{1}\big)\,d_{\mathbf{u}_J} f|_{J}(\mathbf{u}_J),
$$
a sum of $2^{d}-1$ face integrals of the local discrepancy against the mixed differentials of the face
restrictions; bounding each by $\sup|\Delta_N|=D_N^{*}$ times the corresponding Vitali variation and
summing yields @eq-qmc-kh with $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)$ from @eq-qmc-hk. The multivariate Hardy-Krause identity
and the discrepancy rate $D_N^{*}=O((\log N)^d/N)$ for low-discrepancy sequences are classical; we cite
Niederreiter (1992, Chapters 2 and 4) for the full development and do not reproduce the multidimensional
integration-by-parts bookkeeping here. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and what the multidimensional identity says.** The inequality @eq-qmc-kh is the
theorem that licenses the entire QMC program of ML-NMR: it promises that if we spread the covariate nodes
evenly (small $D_N^{*}$) and the response-probability integrand is not pathological (finite
$V_{\mathrm{HK}}$), then the aggregate mean $\theta_{\bullet jk}$ we compute is close to the truth by a
margin we can name in advance, node by node, with no appeal to chance. The realized error on a specific
Sobol' net is genuinely bounded, not merely bounded on average. As for the multidimensional identity we did
not prove in full: it says the integration error decomposes into $2^{d}-1$ contributions, one for each
nonempty subset of coordinates, and each contribution is the local discrepancy integrated against the
roughness of $f$ on the corresponding face of the cube. Geometrically, the whole-cube term ($J=\{1,\dots,d\}$)
charges for how the points fail to fill the interior weighted by how much $f$ twists across it, while the
lower-dimensional terms charge for the same failure restricted to the edges and faces where some coordinates
are pinned to the anchor. Summing all $2^{d}-1$ charges and bounding each by $D_N^{*}$ times a Vitali
variation reassembles the Hardy-Krause variation and gives @eq-qmc-kh. The reader who wants the bookkeeping
will find it in Niederreiter; the reader who wants the moral has it already: error is unevenness times
roughness. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Deterministic, not probabilistic.** The contrast with @thm-mc-rmse is sharp. Monte Carlo gives a
probabilistic statement, a variance and a limiting normal law; the realized error on any one point set is
random. Koksma-Hlawka gives a deterministic, worst-case ceiling on the error of a specific point set,
factored cleanly into a property of the integrand, $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)$, and a property of the points,
$D_N^{*}$. The factorization is what lets ML-NMR fix the points once and reason about the error of the
resulting deterministic likelihood approximation (@def-integration-error-monitoring of Chapter 24 turns the
$N$-versus-$N/2$ comparison into a practical convergence check). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**When the integrand misbehaves.** The bound @eq-qmc-kh is only as good as $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)$ is finite,
and the ML-NMR pullback integrand $\psi$ of @eq-qmc-pullback can have infinite Hardy-Krause variation in
three ways. The first is a discrete covariate margin. If covariate $i$ is binary or ordinal, its inverse
distribution function $F_{j,i}^{-1}$ is a step function, so $\psi$ jumps. A jump along a coordinate
hyperplane keeps the variation finite, but once the copula correlates the discrete covariate with others
the jump surface is tilted, and a jump across a surface not aligned with the axes has infinite
Hardy-Krause variation (@exm-qmc-discrete-jump). The second is an unbounded integrand, for instance a log
link with $\eta$ unbounded on the support, where $g^{-1}=\exp$ grows without bound. The third is subtler
and affects even the logit: with unbounded (for example normal) margins in $d\ge2$ dimensions, the map
$\Phi^{-1}$ inside $T$ has derivatives that blow up at the faces of the cube, and the mixed derivative of
$\psi$ is then not integrable. For instance, with two independent standard normal covariates and
$\eta=a+bz_1+cz_2$, the Vitali variation is
$\int_{\mathbb R^2}|bc\,\mathrm{expit}''(a+bz_1+cz_2)|\,dz_1dz_2=\infty$, since the integrand is constant
along the lines $bz_1+cz_2=\text{const}$. For such integrands the Koksma-Hlawka bound is vacuous, and the
near-$1/N$ behavior seen in practice is justified instead by boundary-growth analyses, which give an error
of order $N^{-1+\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ when the points keep away from the boundary of the
cube (@owen2006halton), or by randomized QMC, in which the deterministic net is randomly scrambled (Owen,
1998), with probabilistic rather than deterministic guarantees. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-qmc-discrete-jump}
## A discrete margin makes the integrand jump
Take the biomarker covariate of the running example (@exm-qmc-psoriasis) alone: binary $X$ with
$P(X=1)=0.3$, so its distribution function is the step $F(x)=0.7$ on $[0,1)$ and $F(x)=1$ on $[1,\infty)$,
and its quantile function is $F^{-1}(u)=0$ for $u\le 0.7$ and $F^{-1}(u)=1$ for $u>0.7$. On an arm with
linear predictor $\eta(x)=-0.5+x$, the cube integrand $\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}(-0.5+F^{-1}(u))$ is flat, then
jumps:

| $u$ | $F^{-1}(u)$ | $\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}(-0.5+F^{-1}(u))$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0.20$ | $0$ | $0.3775$ |
| $0.50$ | $0$ | $0.3775$ |
| $0.70$ | $0$ | $0.3775$ |
| $0.75$ | $1$ | $0.6225$ |
| $0.90$ | $1$ | $0.6225$ |

The integrand cliff-jumps by $0.6225-0.3775=0.2450$ across $u=0.7$. In one dimension this single jump still
has finite total variation ($0.2450$), so the Koksma-Hlawka bound survives and QMC works, though it loses
its edge over evenly spaced grids near the cliff. The real damage is dimensional. When this binary covariate
is correlated with a continuous covariate through the Gaussian copula (@sec-qmc-gaussian), the correlating
step tilts the jump surface off the coordinate axis, and a jump across a tilted surface has *infinite*
Hardy-Krause variation (Owen, 2005): the bound @eq-qmc-kh then reads $|\text{error}|\le\infty$ and promises
nothing. This is precisely the misbehavior flagged above, and the practical fix, randomized (scrambled)
Sobol' nets, recovers good average-case accuracy at the cost of the deterministic guarantee.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Sobol' sequences as digital nets {#sec-qmc-sobol}

The Koksma-Hlawka inequality is only useful if we can exhibit point sets whose star discrepancy actually
attains the low-discrepancy rate $O((\log N)^{d}/N)$. The construction used by ML-NMR software is the
Sobol' sequence (@sobol1967). Its design principle is that the points should be perfectly equidistributed
not merely overall but within every box of a family of dyadic boxes at once; the formalization of "perfect
equidistribution in dyadic boxes" is the digital net.

Before the construction, the four properties a user actually relies on. A Sobol' sequence is **deterministic**
(the same points every time, so the likelihood is reproducible), **evenly spread** (low discrepancy, so the
average converges fast), **nested** (the first $N/2$ points are a subset of the first $N$, so doubling the
node count reuses all previous work and lets the $N$-versus-$N/2$ convergence check of @sec-qmc-example
compare like with like), and **cheap to generate** (each point is a handful of bitwise operations). Two
further practical reasons pick Sobol' over the other classical low-discrepancy families (Halton, Faure,
Niederreiter): Joe and Kuo (2008) published well-tested direction numbers up to dimension $21{,}201$, far
beyond any ML-NMR need, and standard software ships such tables (`multinma` draws its points with the
`randtoolbox` R package), so the covariate nodes are reproducible across machines. The construction below is
optional reading; a user who trusts the software can take the four properties above and skip to
@sec-qmc-pit.

The definition uses one piece of algebra worth naming in advance. $\mathbb{F}_2=\{0,1\}$ is the field of two
elements, where addition is exclusive-or (XOR: $1\oplus 1=0$) and multiplication is the ordinary product; a
**primitive polynomial** over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is, loosely, an irreducible polynomial whose powers cycle
through all nonzero remainders, the algebraic device that guarantees the direction numbers it generates do
not fall into a short repeating pattern and so keep the coordinate well spread. One caution for anyone
implementing the recurrence below: the multiplications by $2$ and by $2^{\ell}$ are ordinary integer
multiplications, and only the combining operation $\oplus$ is over $\mathbb{F}_2$; mixing the two up is the
classic implementation bug.

::: {#def-sobol-net}
## Digital $(t,m,s)$-nets and the Sobol' sequence
Fix a base $b\ge 2$ and a dimension $s$. An **elementary interval** (a $b$-adic box) in $[0,1)^{s}$ is a
product
$$
E=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\Big[\frac{a_i}{b^{d_i}},\frac{a_i+1}{b^{d_i}}\Big),
\qquad d_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},\quad 0\le a_i<b^{d_i},
$$
of volume $b^{-(d_1+\cdots+d_s)}$. A **$(t,m,s)$-net in base $b$** is a set of $N=b^{m}$ points in
$[0,1)^{s}$ such that every elementary interval of volume $b^{t-m}$ (equivalently with
$d_1+\cdots+d_s=m-t$) contains exactly $b^{t}$ of the points. The parameter $t$ measures the deviation from
perfect balance: $t=0$ is ideal, and smaller $t$ is better.

The **Sobol' sequence** is the case $b=2$, built coordinate by coordinate from algebra over the field
$\mathbb{F}_2=\{0,1\}$. For dimension $i$, fix a primitive polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_2$,
$$
p_i(x)=x^{e_i}+a_{i,1}x^{e_i-1}+\cdots+a_{i,e_i-1}x+1,\qquad a_{i,\ell}\in\{0,1\},
$$
of degree $e_i$, and a set of odd initial **direction numbers** $v_{i,\ell}=m_{i,\ell}\,2^{-\ell}$ with
$m_{i,\ell}$ an odd integer below $2^{\ell}$ for $\ell=1,\dots,e_i$. Extend the direction numbers by the
recurrence read off from the polynomial,
$$
m_{i,\ell}=2\,a_{i,1}\,m_{i,\ell-1}\oplus 2^{2}a_{i,2}\,m_{i,\ell-2}\oplus\cdots
\oplus 2^{e_i}m_{i,\ell-e_i}\oplus m_{i,\ell-e_i},\qquad \ell>e_i,
$$
where $\oplus$ is bitwise exclusive-or. The $i$-th coordinate of the $n$-th Sobol' point is the
exclusive-or of the direction numbers selected by the binary digits of $n=\sum_{\ell\ge 1}b_{\ell}2^{\ell-1}$,
$$
u_{n,i}=\bigoplus_{\ell:\,b_\ell=1} v_{i,\ell}.
$$ {#eq-qmc-sobol-point}
With suitable direction numbers (Joe and Kuo, 2008), the Sobol' points form a $(t,m,s)$-net in base $2$ for
$N=2^{m}$ and achieve the low-discrepancy rate $D_N^{*}=O\big((\log N)^{s}/N\big)$ (@sobol1967). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The first coordinate is the van der Corput sequence.** Taking the trivial direction numbers
$v_{1,\ell}=2^{-\ell}$ in @eq-qmc-sobol-point gives, in dimension one, $u_{n,1}=\sum_{\ell:b_\ell=1}2^{-\ell}$,
which is exactly the radical-inverse (van der Corput) sequence in base $2$: it reflects the binary digits
of $n$ about the radix point. For $n=1,2,3,4,5,6,7$ this produces
$$
\tfrac12,\ \tfrac14,\ \tfrac34,\ \tfrac18,\ \tfrac58,\ \tfrac38,\ \tfrac78,
$$
which as a set is precisely $\{\tfrac18,\tfrac28,\tfrac38,\tfrac48,\tfrac58,\tfrac68,\tfrac78\}$, the seven
interior eighths. One checks directly that this seven-point set has star discrepancy $D_7^{*}=\tfrac18$,
close to $1/N$, whereas a typical set of seven independent uniform points has discrepancy of order
$1/\sqrt 7\approx 0.38$. The contrast is the QMC advantage in miniature, and we use exactly these points in
the worked example of @sec-qmc-example. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What scrambling is, in one paragraph.** We invoke "randomized" or "scrambled" Sobol' nets twice as the
remedy for integrands of unbounded variation (discrete margins, @exm-qmc-discrete-jump) and for very high
dimension. Scrambling, due to Owen (1998), applies a random but structure-preserving relabeling of the
digits of every coordinate of every point: the dyadic-box balance that makes a Sobol' net low-discrepancy is
kept exactly, but the specific point positions are randomized. The payoff is twofold. First, one now has a
family of statistically identical nets, so averaging the estimate over a few independent scrambles yields an
honest, MC-style error bar for the integration error even though each net is deterministic once drawn.
Second, for smooth integrands the scrambling improves the rate to nearly $N^{-3/2}$, and for the rough
integrands where plain QMC lost its guarantee it restores near-optimal accuracy in an average-case sense.
The cost is that the deterministic, worst-case Koksma-Hlawka ceiling is traded for a probabilistic one; for
the central inference of an HTA this is usually a good trade. A scrambled net is still fixed once per fit,
so the smoothness in the parameters that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo needs is preserved. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The probability integral transform {#sec-qmc-pit}

We now turn from the cube to the covariate space, and to the construction of the transport map $T$ of
@eq-qmc-pullback. Here is where this section is headed, stated before the theorems so the pieces have a
purpose: to turn a uniform Sobol' input into a covariate value we will invert that covariate's marginal
distribution function, and the theorem below guarantees that inverting the CDF of a uniform input reproduces
exactly the intended distribution. Concretely, take age in the running example (@exm-qmc-psoriasis),
modeled as $\mathcal{N}(45,12^{2})$. Its quantile function $F^{-1}$ turns a uniform number into an age:
$F^{-1}(0.5)=45$ (the median), $F^{-1}(0.975)=45+1.96\cdot 12\approx 68.5$, $F^{-1}(0.025)\approx 21.5$. Feed
in uniform inputs spread across $(0,1)$ and the ages that come out are distributed exactly as
$\mathcal{N}(45,12^{2})$. The same device handles the biomarker: with $P(X=1)=0.3$ the quantile function
returns $0$ for inputs up to $0.7$ and $1$ above, so $30\%$ of uniform inputs map to biomarker-positive, as
intended. The atom of the construction is therefore the probability integral transform: the fact that any
distribution can be generated from a uniform random number by applying the inverse distribution function,
and conversely that a continuous distribution function maps its own variable back to uniform. We use the
generalized inverse so that the statements hold for arbitrary, not only strictly increasing, distribution
functions, which is what lets the biomarker's step function participate.

::: {#lem-quantile-galois}
## The quantile coupling inequality
Let $F:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ be a distribution function, that is nondecreasing and right-continuous with
$F(-\infty)=0$ and $F(+\infty)=1$, and define its **generalized inverse** (the quantile function)
$$
F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)\ge u\},\qquad u\in(0,1).
$$
Then for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and $u\in(0,1)$,
$$
F^{-1}(u)\le x\iff u\le F(x).
$$ {#eq-qmc-galois}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $A_u=\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$, so $F^{-1}(u)=\inf A_u$. Because $F$ is nondecreasing, $A_u$ is an upper set:
if $x\in A_u$ and $x'\ge x$ then $x'\in A_u$. Because $F$ is right-continuous, $A_u$ is closed on the left,
hence contains its infimum: taking $x_m\downarrow F^{-1}(u)$ with $x_m\in A_u$, right-continuity gives
$F(F^{-1}(u))=\lim_m F(x_m)\ge u$, so $F^{-1}(u)\in A_u$ and $A_u=[F^{-1}(u),\infty)$.

($\Leftarrow$) If $u\le F(x)$ then $x\in A_u$, so $x\ge\inf A_u=F^{-1}(u)$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $F^{-1}(u)\le x$ then, by monotonicity and $F^{-1}(u)\in A_u$,
$F(x)\ge F(F^{-1}(u))\ge u$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-inverse-cdf}
## Inverse-CDF transformation
Let $F$ be a distribution function and $F^{-1}$ its generalized inverse.

1. **(Inverse transform.)** If $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, then $F^{-1}(U)\sim F$.

2. **(Probability integral transform.)** If, in addition, $F$ is continuous and $X\sim F$, then
$F(X)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* For any $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the coupling inequality @eq-qmc-galois gives the event identity
$\{F^{-1}(U)\le x\}=\{U\le F(x)\}$. Since $U$ is uniform and $F(x)\in[0,1]$,
$$
P\big(F^{-1}(U)\le x\big)=P\big(U\le F(x)\big)=F(x).
$$
Thus $F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution function $F$, that is $F^{-1}(U)\sim F$.

*Part 2.* Fix $u\in(0,1)$ and set $x_u=\sup\{x:F(x)\le u\}$. Continuity of $F$ gives $F(x_u)=u$: indeed
$F\to 0,1$ at $\mp\infty$ and $F$ is continuous, so by the intermediate value theorem the level $u$ is
attained, and $x_u$ is the largest point of attainment. We claim the event identity
$\{F(X)\le u\}=\{X\le x_u\}$. If $X\le x_u$ then $F(X)\le F(x_u)=u$ by monotonicity. Conversely, if
$X>x_u$ then, $x_u$ being the supremum of $\{F\le u\}$, every $t>x_u$ has $F(t)>u$, so $F(X)>u$; contrapositively
$F(X)\le u$ forces $X\le x_u$. Therefore
$$
P\big(F(X)\le u\big)=P\big(X\le x_u\big)=F(x_u)=u\qquad\text{for every }u\in(0,1),
$$
which is the distribution function of $\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. Hence $F(X)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Continuity is essential for the forward map.** Part 1 needs no continuity: the inverse transform
generates any distribution, discrete or continuous, from a uniform draw, and this is the workhorse of
random-variate generation. Part 2 fails for discrete $F$: if $X$ is Bernoulli with success probability
$\pi$, then $F(X)$ takes only the two values $1-\pi$ (when $X=0$) and $1$ (when $X=1$), so $F(X)$ is not
uniform. This asymmetry is exactly the source of the discrete-margin caveat in @thm-koksma-hlawka: a
discrete covariate enters the pipeline through Part 1 only, its inverse distribution function is a step
function, and the resulting jumps inflate the Hardy-Krause variation of the integrand. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Sklar's theorem {#sec-qmc-sklar}

The inverse-CDF transform handles one covariate at a time. To build a joint covariate law from the
marginal summaries that an AgD study reports, we need a principled way to glue marginals together with a
specified dependence. Here is the concrete gap. The running example's aggregate arm (@exm-qmc-psoriasis)
reports a mean age and a mean baseline severity, which fix each covariate's own distribution, but says
nothing about how they are paired within patients: do older patients tend to be more severe, or is there no
association? Two arms with identical margins but different age-severity pairing have different covariate
clouds, and, because the response probability bends nonlinearly with the linear predictor, different
aggregate means. The margins alone do not determine the integral; we must supply the pairing.

One might ask why we do not simply assume the covariates are jointly normal and be done. The answer is that
real covariates are not all normal: the biomarker is binary, and severity or duration may be skewed or
bounded. A joint normal would force a normal margin on the biomarker, which is nonsense for a $0/1$ variable.
What we want is to keep a sensible margin for each covariate (normal age, normal severity, Bernoulli
biomarker) and glue them with a chosen dependence, without the dependence disturbing the margins. Sklar's
theorem is exactly that principle: it asserts that every joint distribution factors into its marginals and a
single object, the copula, that carries all of the dependence and none of the marginal information, so
margin and dependence can be chosen separately and then combined.

::: {#def-copula}
## Copula
A function $C:[0,1]^{d}\to[0,1]$ is a **$d$-dimensional copula** if it is the joint distribution function
of a random vector $(U_1,\dots,U_d)$ each of whose components is uniform on $[0,1]$. Equivalently, $C$ is
grounded ($C(\mathbf{u})=0$ if any $u_i=0$), has uniform one-dimensional margins
($C(1,\dots,1,u_i,1,\dots,1)=u_i$), and is $d$-increasing (the $C$-measure of every box in $[0,1]^d$ is
nonnegative). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: a copula is dependence with the units stripped off.** Push each covariate through its
own CDF and it becomes uniform on $[0,1]$ (the probability integral transform, @thm-inverse-cdf), the same
for every covariate regardless of its original scale. What survives that rescaling is only the pattern of
association, and the copula $C$ is precisely the joint distribution of those rescaled uniforms. So a copula
answers "which quantiles tend to occur together", for example "do high-age-percentile patients tend to be
high-severity-percentile patients", with the marginal scales of age and severity deliberately discarded. It
is dependence in pure form, ready to be reattached to any margins we like. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-copula-lipschitz}
## Copulas are Lipschitz
Every $d$-copula $C$ is $1$-Lipschitz in the $\ell^{1}$ sense:
$|C(\mathbf{u})-C(\mathbf{v})|\le\sum_{i=1}^{d}|u_i-v_i|$ for all $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in[0,1]^{d}$. In
particular $C$ is continuous.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $(U_1,\dots,U_d)$ have joint distribution function $C$ with uniform margins, so that
$C(\mathbf{u})=P(\bigcap_i\{U_i\le u_i\})$. For events $A,B$, $|P(A)-P(B)|\le P(A\triangle B)$, where
$A\triangle B$ is the symmetric difference. With $A=\bigcap_i\{U_i\le u_i\}$ and
$B=\bigcap_i\{U_i\le v_i\}$, a point lies in $A\triangle B$ only if for some coordinate $i$ the value
$U_i$ falls between $u_i$ and $v_i$, so
$A\triangle B\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{d}\{\min(u_i,v_i)<U_i\le\max(u_i,v_i)\}$. By the union bound and the
uniform margins, $P(A\triangle B)\le\sum_i P(\min(u_i,v_i)<U_i\le\max(u_i,v_i))=\sum_i|u_i-v_i|$. Hence
$|C(\mathbf{u})-C(\mathbf{v})|\le\sum_i|u_i-v_i|$, and continuity follows. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-sklar}
## Sklar's theorem
Let $F$ be a joint distribution function on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with one-dimensional margins
$F_1,\dots,F_d$. Then there exists a copula $C$ such that
$$
F(x_1,\dots,x_d)=C\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big)\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
$$ {#eq-qmc-sklar}
If the margins $F_1,\dots,F_d$ are all continuous, then $C$ is unique and is given on $[0,1]^{d}$ by
$$
C(u_1,\dots,u_d)=F\big(F_1^{-1}(u_1),\dots,F_d^{-1}(u_d)\big).
$$ {#eq-qmc-sklar-explicit}
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the existence direction in the continuous case; this is the case used by ML-NMR, where every
covariate margin is taken continuous. Let $(X_1,\dots,X_d)\sim F$. Because each $F_i$ is continuous,
@thm-inverse-cdf(2) gives $U_i:=F_i(X_i)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. Let $C$ be the joint distribution function
of $(U_1,\dots,U_d)$. Its one-dimensional margins are the laws of the $U_i$, each uniform, so $C$ is a
copula by @def-copula.

It remains to verify the factorization @eq-qmc-sklar. From the proof of @thm-inverse-cdf(2), for each $i$
and each $u_i\in(0,1)$ the event identity $\{F_i(X_i)\le u_i\}=\{X_i\le x_{i,u_i}\}$ holds with
$x_{i,u_i}=\sup\{x:F_i(x)\le u_i\}$ and $F_i(x_{i,u_i})=u_i$. Intersecting over the coordinates,
$$
C(u_1,\dots,u_d)=P\Big(\bigcap_{i=1}^{d}\{F_i(X_i)\le u_i\}\Big)
=P\Big(\bigcap_{i=1}^{d}\{X_i\le x_{i,u_i}\}\Big)=F(x_{1,u_1},\dots,x_{d,u_d}).
$$ {#eq-qmc-sklar-step}
Now evaluate @eq-qmc-sklar-step at $u_i=F_i(x_i)$ for a given $\mathbf{x}$. Then
$x_{i,F_i(x_i)}=\sup\{t:F_i(t)\le F_i(x_i)\}\ge x_i$, and $F_i$ is flat at level $F_i(x_i)$ on the interval
$[x_i,x_{i,F_i(x_i)}]$, so $F_i(x_{i,F_i(x_i)})=F_i(x_i)$ and the coordinate-$i$ enlargement
$\{x_i<X_i\le x_{i,F_i(x_i)}\}$ has probability $F_i(x_{i,F_i(x_i)})-F_i(x_i)=0$. Enlarging each coordinate
adds a null set, and a finite union of null sets is null, so the joint probability is unchanged:
$F(x_{1,F_1(x_1)},\dots,x_{d,F_d(x_d)})=F(x_1,\dots,x_d)$. Combined with @eq-qmc-sklar-step at
$u_i=F_i(x_i)$ this gives $C(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d))=F(\mathbf{x})$, which is @eq-qmc-sklar.

*Uniqueness and the explicit form.* When the margins are continuous, each $F_i$ has range all of
$[0,1]$, so as $x_i$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$ the argument $u_i=F_i(x_i)$ ranges over $(0,1)$; thus
@eq-qmc-sklar pins down $C$ on a dense subset of $[0,1]^{d}$, and by @lem-copula-lipschitz $C$ is
continuous, so it is determined on all of $[0,1]^{d}$, proving uniqueness. Finally, putting
$u_i\in(0,1)$ into @eq-qmc-sklar-step and using $x_{i,u_i}=F_i^{-1}(u_i)$ for continuous $F_i$ (the largest
and smallest points attaining level $u_i$ differ only across a flat, on which $X_i$ has zero probability)
gives @eq-qmc-sklar-explicit. $\square$
:::

::: {#cor-margins-copula-determine}
## Margins plus copula determine the distribution
Let $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}'$ be random vectors on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with the same continuous
one-dimensional margins $F_1,\dots,F_d$ and the same copula $C$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}'$ have
the same joint distribution. Equivalently, a continuous joint law is completely specified by naming its
margins and its copula.
:::

::: {.proof}
By Sklar's theorem (@thm-sklar), the joint distribution function of $\mathbf{X}$ is
$F(\mathbf{x})=C(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d))$, and that of $\mathbf{X}'$ is the same expression with the same
$C$ and the same $F_i$; hence the two distribution functions are identical, and a distribution on
$\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is determined by its distribution function. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation, and why we isolate it.** This one-line corollary is the license for the whole ML-NMR
construction: to specify a synthetic covariate distribution it is *enough* to choose each margin and choose
a copula, and no further information is needed or possible. We pull it out as a named result because the
integration pipeline (@thm-hypercube-integration) leans on it at its crux, where it must conclude that a
vector built to have the study's margins and the study's copula is distributed exactly as the study
covariates $f_j$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why Sklar is the right tool for aggregate data.** Sklar's theorem says exactly what an AgD study does and
does not constrain. The reported marginal summaries fix the margins $F_1,\dots,F_d$, for instance a normal
margin for a continuous biomarker calibrated to its reported mean and standard deviation, or a beta margin
for a proportion. They say nothing about the copula $C$. ML-NMR therefore supplies $C$ from outside the AgD
study, most often as a Gaussian copula whose correlation matrix is borrowed from the IPD study in the
network or from external evidence (@sec-qmc-gaussian). The factorization @eq-qmc-sklar guarantees that any
choice of copula combined with the fixed margins yields a legitimate joint distribution with exactly those
margins, so the marginal calibration is never disturbed by the dependence assumption. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The Gaussian copula {#sec-qmc-gaussian}

The default copula for ML-NMR is the Gaussian copula: take a multivariate normal vector with a specified
correlation matrix, and read off its dependence through the probability integral transform. It is the
copula of a multivariate normal, stripped of its margins.

::: {#def-gaussian-copula}
## Gaussian copula
Let $\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succeq 0$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal (a
correlation matrix). The **Gaussian copula** with correlation matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is
$$
C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(u_1,\dots,u_d)
=\Phi_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d)\big),
$$ {#eq-qmc-gaussian-copula}
where $\Phi_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is the joint distribution function of $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$
and $\Phi^{-1}$ is the standard normal quantile function. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: borrow the dependence of a normal, keep your own margins.** A multivariate normal has
a familiar dependence structure, one correlation number per pair of variables. The Gaussian copula is that
dependence structure with the normal margins peeled away, ready to be glued onto whatever margins the
covariates actually have. Operationally: to correlate the covariates, first pretend they are standard
normals with correlation $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, generate correlated normal draws, then convert each back to
its true margin. The correlation matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is the one free input, and in ML-NMR it is
borrowed from the IPD study in the network (or from external evidence) because an AgD study never reports
it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula}
## The Gaussian copula is a copula, with an explicit sampler
The function @eq-qmc-gaussian-copula is a copula. Moreover, if $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$
and $U_i=\Phi(Z_i)$, then $(U_1,\dots,U_d)$ has distribution function $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$; and if
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}=LL^{\top}$ is a Cholesky factorization and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_d)$,
then $\mathbf{Z}=L\boldsymbol{\zeta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$. The diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is
unity, so each $Z_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and since $\Phi$ is continuous, @thm-inverse-cdf(2) gives
$U_i=\Phi(Z_i)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. The joint distribution function of $\mathbf{U}=(U_1,\dots,U_d)$ is,
using that $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing so $\{\Phi(Z_i)\le u_i\}=\{Z_i\le\Phi^{-1}(u_i)\}$,
$$
P\Big(\bigcap_{i}\{U_i\le u_i\}\Big)=P\Big(\bigcap_i\{Z_i\le\Phi^{-1}(u_i)\}\Big)
=\Phi_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d)\big)=C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\mathbf{u}).
$$
Thus $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is the joint distribution function of $\mathbf{U}$, whose margins are
uniform; it is a copula by @def-copula, and $\mathbf{U}=\Phi(\mathbf{Z})$ samples it. For the last claim,
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is a correlation matrix hence positive semidefinite (the covariance-matrix
positivity of @thm-cov-psd), so it admits a Cholesky factor $L$; the linear image
$\mathbf{Z}=L\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ of a standard normal vector is normal with mean $\mathbf{0}$ and
covariance $L I_d L^{\top}=LL^{\top}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}$. $\square$
:::

Combining @prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula with Sklar's theorem and the inverse-CDF transform gives the
construction of a joint covariate law from marginal summaries and a correlation matrix.

::: {.remark}
**From a Gaussian copula to any margins.** Given target margins $F_1,\dots,F_d$ and a correlation matrix
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, sample $\mathbf{X}$ with those margins and Gaussian-copula dependence by: drawing
$\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$; setting $U_i=\Phi(Z_i)$ (uniforms with the
Gaussian copula, @prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula); and setting $X_i=F_i^{-1}(U_i)$ (the inverse transform,
@thm-inverse-cdf(1)). By Sklar's theorem (@thm-sklar) the resulting $\mathbf{X}$ has exactly the margins
$F_i$ and copula $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. The correlation $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is the correlation of the
latent normals, not in general of $\mathbf{X}$ itself; the two coincide only when the margins are
themselves normal, and otherwise are linked through the margins by a monotone transformation that preserves
rank correlations. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Which correlation is which: a caution against pasting in a trial table.** The single most common misuse of
this machinery is to read a Pearson correlation off a trial's covariate table and drop it straight into
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$. That is wrong unless the covariates are themselves normal, because $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$
is the correlation of the *latent* normals, not of the covariates. Four distinct quantities are in play, and
keeping them apart is essential.

| Quantity | What it is | Preserved by the Gaussian copula? |
|---|---|---|
| Latent correlation $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ | Pearson correlation of the underlying normal scores $\mathbf{Z}$ | this is the input you set |
| Covariate Pearson correlation | linear correlation of the covariates $\mathbf{X}$ themselves | no: equals $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ only for normal margins, else attenuated |
| Spearman rank correlation | correlation of the covariate ranks (quantiles) | yes: unchanged by any monotone remargining |
| Tail dependence | tendency to be jointly extreme in the tails | always zero for a Gaussian copula |

The safe practice is to convert. For continuous margins the Spearman correlation $\rho^{S}$ of two covariates
equals that of their latent normals, and a normal pair with Spearman correlation $\rho^{S}$ has Pearson
correlation $2\sin(\pi\rho^{S}/6)$, so setting $\Omega_{ik}=2\sin(\pi\rho^{S}_{ik}/6)$ from the IPD rank
correlations reproduces them; `multinma` applies such adjustments by default. Pasting in the reported
Pearson values instead is a mild misspecification, and the realized covariate correlations after non-normal
margins will be somewhat attenuated. @exr-qmc-gaussian-copula-cov makes this attenuation quantitative. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Evaluating versus sampling the copula.** The defining formula @eq-qmc-gaussian-copula contains the
multivariate normal distribution function $\Phi_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$, which has no elementary closed form
for $d\ge 2$; in the bivariate case it reduces to Owen's $T$-function and the tabulated bivariate normal
integral (@owen1956), and for $d\ge 3$ it is itself computed by numerical integration. Crucially, the
ML-NMR pipeline never needs to evaluate $\Phi_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. It needs only to sample from the
copula, and sampling proceeds through the Cholesky route of @prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula, which touches
only the standard univariate $\Phi$ and the factorization of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$. This is why a $d$-variate
dependence can be imposed at the cost of a single $d\times d$ Cholesky factorization. The Gaussian copula
also has zero tail dependence, so it understates the chance of two covariates being jointly extreme; for
the central inference of HTA this is usually acceptable, and a $t$-copula or vine copula is the remedy when
it is not. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What tail dependence is, and when to worry.** Tail dependence asks: given that one covariate is extreme,
how likely is another to be extreme too? Formally it is the limiting conditional probability
$\lim_{q\to 1}P\big(X_2>F_2^{-1}(q)\mid X_1>F_1^{-1}(q)\big)$, the chance of a joint upper extreme. The
Gaussian copula sends this limit to $0$ for every correlation $\boldsymbol{\Omega}\ne\mathbf{1}$: no matter
how strongly two covariates are correlated in the bulk, the Gaussian copula treats their simultaneous
extremes as asymptotically independent. Clinically, this can understate reality when severe risk factors
cluster: a patient in the worst decile of baseline severity may be far more likely than a Gaussian copula
predicts to also be in the worst decile of, say, inflammatory burden, and if both are strong effect
modifiers the aggregate response probability in that jointly severe corner is mis-weighted. When the
decision hinges on such a corner, a $t$-copula (which has positive, symmetric tail dependence) or a vine
copula (which lets each pair have its own tail behavior) is the principled replacement; for most central
HTA estimates, where the bulk of the covariate mass drives the integral, the Gaussian copula's convenience
outweighs its blindness to the tails. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The ML-NMR integration pipeline {#sec-qmc-pipeline}

We can now assemble the transport map $T$ and prove the error bound for the aggregation integral. The
pipeline reads as a chain of the transforms just developed: Sobol' points into the cube, inverse normal to
get independent normals, Cholesky to correlate them, normal distribution function back to uniforms with the
Gaussian copula, and target inverse-CDFs to land on the covariate margins.

Before the theorem, the same pipeline as a recipe a practitioner can follow. Given the study's marginal
distributions $F_{j,1},\dots,F_{j,d}$, its correlation matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ with Cholesky factor
$L$, and a chosen number of nodes $N$:

1. **Choose points.** Take the first $N$ Sobol' points $\mathbf{u}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{u}^{(N)}$ in the unit
   cube $[0,1]^{d}$ (evenly spread, deterministic, nested).
2. **To independent normals.** Apply the inverse normal CDF coordinatewise, $\mathbf{z}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf{u})$,
   turning each point into a vector of independent standard normal scores.
3. **Correlate.** Multiply by the Cholesky factor, $\tilde{\mathbf{z}}=L\mathbf{z}$, giving normal scores
   with the target correlation $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$.
4. **Back to uniforms.** Apply the normal CDF coordinatewise, $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\Phi(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})$,
   giving uniforms carrying the Gaussian-copula dependence.
5. **To covariate values.** Apply each covariate's quantile function, $x_i=F_{j,i}^{-1}(\tilde u_i)$,
   landing on a synthetic covariate profile with the right margins and the right dependence.
6. **Evaluate the model.** Compute the individual response probability
   $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}))$ at each profile.
7. **Average.** The mean of those $N$ predictions is the estimate $\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}$ of the
   aggregate mean.

Steps 1 to 5 build the transport map $T$ and the fixed covariate nodes $\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})$;
they use only the study's reported summaries and are done once, before the fit begins. Only steps 6 and 7
depend on the model parameters and are recomputed as the sampler explores the posterior. The theorem now
states this precisely and bounds the error of step 7.

::: {#thm-hypercube-integration}
## Integration over the unit hypercube
Let study $j$ have covariate density $f_j$ with continuous marginal distribution functions
$F_{j,1},\dots,F_{j,d}$ and Gaussian-copula correlation matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j=L L^{\top}$. Define
the transport map $T:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathcal{X}$ coordinatewise by
$$
\mathbf{z}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf{u}),\quad
\tilde{\mathbf{z}}=L\mathbf{z},\quad
\tilde u_i=\Phi(\tilde z_i),\quad
x_i=F_{j,i}^{-1}(\tilde u_i),\qquad T(\mathbf{u})=(x_1,\dots,x_d),
$$ {#eq-qmc-pipeline}
