where $\Phi^{-1}$ and $\Phi$ act componentwise. Then:

1. **(Correctness.)** If $\mathbf{U}\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{d})$, then $\mathbf{X}=T(\mathbf{U})\sim f_j$;
that is, $T$ pushes the uniform law on the cube forward to the covariate law $f_j$. Consequently the
aggregation integral @eq-qmc-aggregation equals the cube integral of the pullback $\psi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_{jk}\circ T$,
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\psi(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u}.
$$ {#eq-qmc-pipeline-pullback}

2. **(Quasi-Monte Carlo estimate and error.)** For a point set $P_N=\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}\subset[0,1]^{d}$
the estimate $\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})$ obeys, whenever
$V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)<\infty$,
$$
\big|\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}-\theta_{\bullet jk}\big|\le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\,D_N^{*}(P_N).
$$ {#eq-qmc-pipeline-error}
With $P_N$ a Sobol' net (@def-sobol-net), $D_N^{*}(P_N)=O((\log N)^{d}/N)$, so the integration error is
$O\big(V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)(\log N)^{d}/N\big)$. Finite variation holds for $d=1$ with a continuous margin
and a bounded monotone integrand (then $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\le 1$), but not automatically for $d\ge2$
with unbounded margins, where the bound can be vacuous (the remark "When the integrand misbehaves" in
@sec-qmc-koksma).
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Track a uniform input through @eq-qmc-pipeline. Let $\mathbf{U}\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{d})$ with
independent coordinates. By @thm-inverse-cdf(1) applied to $F=\Phi$, each $Z_i=\Phi^{-1}(U_i)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$,
and independence is preserved coordinatewise, so $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_d)$. The linear
map gives $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}=L\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},LL^{\top})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j)$
(@prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula). Setting $\tilde U_i=\Phi(\tilde Z_i)$ then yields, by the same
proposition, a vector $\tilde{\mathbf{U}}=(\tilde U_1,\dots,\tilde U_d)$ with uniform margins and joint law
the Gaussian copula $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j}$. Finally $X_i=F_{j,i}^{-1}(\tilde U_i)$ has, by
@thm-inverse-cdf(1), marginal distribution function $F_{j,i}$, and by Sklar's theorem (@thm-sklar) the
vector $\mathbf{X}$ has copula $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j}$; a distribution is determined by its margins and
its copula (@cor-margins-copula-determine), so $\mathbf{X}\sim f_j$. Therefore $T$ pushes $\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{d})$ forward to $f_j$, and
the change-of-variables identity for the pushforward measure, applied to $\varphi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_{jk}$,
gives
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{U}}\big[\varphi(T(\mathbf{U}))\big]
=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\varphi(T(\mathbf{u}))\,d\mathbf{u}=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\psi(\mathbf{u})\,d\mathbf{u},
$$
which is @eq-qmc-pipeline-pullback.

*Part 2.* Apply the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (@thm-koksma-hlawka) to the integrand $\psi$ on $[0,1]^{d}$
with the point set $P_N$: the left-hand side of @eq-qmc-kh is exactly
$|\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}-\theta_{\bullet jk}|$ by @eq-qmc-pipeline-pullback, giving
@eq-qmc-pipeline-error. The Sobol' discrepancy rate is @def-sobol-net. For continuous margins each
$F_{j,i}^{-1}$ is continuous and the composed map $T$ is continuous; for the logit link $g^{-1}=\mathrm{expit}$
is smooth and bounded into $(0,1)$, so $\psi$ is continuous and bounded; whether its Hardy-Krause
variation is finite depends on the margins and the dimension, as the final sentence of Part 2 records.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters: the capstone of the chapter.** @thm-hypercube-integration is the whole chapter in one
statement. It takes the only thing an AgD study gives us, marginal summaries and a borrowed correlation, and
delivers the one thing ML-NMR needs, the aggregate response probability $\theta_{\bullet jk}$, with an
error that shrinks at nearly the $1/N$ rate: deterministically when $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)$ is finite, and
by the boundary-growth argument otherwise. Every earlier section is a component: the
inverse-CDF transform is step 5, the Gaussian copula is steps 2 to 4, Sobol' nets are step 1, and
Koksma-Hlawka is the error bound @eq-qmc-pipeline-error. The payoff for indirect comparison is direct: this
$\theta_{\bullet jk}$, contrasted across arms, is the relative effect the network estimates, so a trustworthy
integral is what makes the odds ratio of one drug versus another, and the HTA recommendation that rests on
it, trustworthy. The same map $T$ evaluated at a target population's margins (@sec-qmc-pipeline, scope
remark below) is what lets ML-NMR report that odds ratio in a population matching neither trial.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The nodes are fixed; the integrand is smooth in the parameters.** The covariate nodes
$\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})$ depend only on the study's margins $F_{j,i}$ and correlation
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$, not on the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\mu_j,\boldsymbol{\beta}_1,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k},\gamma_k,\dots)$.
They are computed once, before sampling begins. The aggregate mean is then the fixed finite average
$$
\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}g^{-1}\!\Big(\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^{(n)\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_1
+\mathbf{x}^{(n)\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2,k}+\gamma_k\Big),
$$ {#eq-qmc-fixed-nodes}
a smooth, deterministic function of $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ with an exact gradient
$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\widehat\theta_{\bullet jk}^{(N)}$ obtained by differentiating the sum term by
term. This is precisely what Hamiltonian Monte Carlo requires (@def-hmc, @carpenter2017stan): a
differentiable log-likelihood. Replacing the fixed Sobol' net by fresh random draws at each step, as plain
Monte Carlo would, would make @eq-qmc-fixed-nodes a noisy function of $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ and break the
gradient, which is the deeper reason QMC, not MC, is the integration rule of ML-NMR
(@thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma builds on this aggregate likelihood, and @def-integration-error-monitoring of
Chapter 24 monitors the residual integration error against the Markov chain Monte Carlo error).
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Scope of the pipeline.** The construction integrates against any joint covariate distribution specified
by continuous margins and a correlation matrix, and so computes the aggregation integral @eq-qmc-aggregation
for any link, including the logit for which no closed form exists (@thm-logit-no-closed-form). The same
pipeline computes the target-population estimand integral (@thm-target-population-integral of Chapter 23) by
substituting the target population's margins and correlation for the study's, which is what lets ML-NMR
report a contrast in a population represented by neither trial. It carries over verbatim to the unanchored
extension of Chapter 26. Randomized (scrambled) Sobol' nets supply error bars when the deterministic guarantee is
vacuous, and vine or $t$ copulas replace the Gaussian copula when its dependence structure is inadequate. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Practical guidance: how to choose $N$ and read the diagnostic.** In an applied analysis the number of
nodes $N$ is not chosen from the Koksma-Hlawka constant, which is unknown, but by a doubling check.
Compute the aggregate mean at $N$ and at $N/2$ nodes; because the Sobol' net is nested, the $N/2$ points are
a subset of the $N$ points and the gap $|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}|$ is a rough proxy for
the remaining integration error: when the error halves at each doubling the gap is about the size of the
error at $N$ (in @exm-qmc-logit it slightly understates it), so a margin of safety is prudent. Double $N$ until this gap falls well below the scale that matters, then stop. What scale
matters? The integration error should be small *relative to the posterior uncertainty* in the same quantity:
there is no value in pinning $\theta_{\bullet jk}$ to five decimals when the posterior credible interval for
the corresponding response rate is $0.1$ wide, and conversely an error of $0.005$ on the probability scale
can matter if a reimbursement decision turns on a hair's-breadth difference between two treatments near a
cost-effectiveness threshold. The workable rule is: the integration error should be an order of magnitude
smaller than both the posterior standard deviation of the estimand and the smallest decision-relevant
difference in the target contrast. Chapter 24 formalizes this comparison, monitoring the integration error
against the Markov chain Monte Carlo error so that neither source dominates
(@def-integration-error-monitoring). The `multinma` default is $N=64$ nodes per study, to be checked by this
kind of comparison; a discrete or skewed covariate, or a near-threshold decision, warrants raising $N$ and
rechecking the gap. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A worked example: a logit aggregate mean by quasi-Monte Carlo {#sec-qmc-example}

We carry the integration pipeline through a logit aggregate mean from start to finish, choosing the inputs
so that every node and every running estimate can be reproduced with a calculator and a short table of
normal quantiles. This is the stripped-down version of the running example (@exm-qmc-psoriasis) promised in
the introduction: read the single covariate $X$ as a standardized baseline severity in the psoriasis arm,
$\mu$ as the arm's treatment effect on the log-odds scale, and $\theta_{\bullet}$ as the modeled response
rate the network will contrast against a comparator. The integral is the binary-outcome aggregate
probability @eq-qmc-aggregation that ML-NMR forms for an AgD arm, and we take a single covariate so that the
copula step is trivial and the arithmetic is transparent; a two-covariate trace afterward exhibits the
copula step explicitly.

::: {#exm-qmc-logit}
## A one-covariate logit aggregate mean
A study $j$ has one continuous covariate with a standard normal margin, $X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and the
arm in question has linear predictor $\eta(x)=\mu+x$ on the logit scale, so the aggregate event probability
is
$$
\theta_{\bullet}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{expit}(\mu+x)\,\phi(x)\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{expit}\big(\mu+\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)\,du,
$$
the second equality being the pullback @eq-qmc-pipeline-pullback with $d=1$, where the pipeline
@eq-qmc-pipeline reduces to $x=F^{-1}(u)=\Phi^{-1}(u)$ (the Cholesky factor is $L=1$ and the two normal
transforms cancel). We use the seven-point Sobol' (van der Corput) set
$\{\tfrac18,\tfrac28,\dots,\tfrac78\}$ of @sec-qmc-sobol, whose nodes carry the standard normal quantiles
$$
\Phi^{-1}\!\Big(\tfrac{k}{8}\Big):\quad
-1.1503,\ -0.6745,\ -0.3186,\ 0,\ 0.3186,\ 0.6745,\ 1.1503\quad(k=1,\dots,7).
$$

**Part A: a symmetric case with a known answer ($\mu=0$).** Here the integrand
$\psi(u)=\mathrm{expit}(\Phi^{-1}(u))$ satisfies $\psi(1-u)=\mathrm{expit}(-\Phi^{-1}(u))=1-\psi(u)$, using
$\Phi^{-1}(1-u)=-\Phi^{-1}(u)$ and $\mathrm{expit}(-z)=1-\mathrm{expit}(z)$; integrating, $\theta_{\bullet}=1-\theta_{\bullet}$,
so the exact value is $\theta_{\bullet}=\tfrac12$. The seven node values are

| $k$ | $x=\Phi^{-1}(k/8)$ | $\mathrm{expit}(x)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $-1.1503$ | $0.2404$ |
| 2 | $-0.6745$ | $0.3375$ |
| 3 | $-0.3186$ | $0.4210$ |
| 4 | $0$ | $0.5000$ |
| 5 | $0.3186$ | $0.5790$ |
| 6 | $0.6745$ | $0.6625$ |
| 7 | $1.1503$ | $0.7596$ |

The values pair as $0.2404+0.7596=0.3375+0.6625=0.4210+0.5790=1$, with the central node contributing
$0.5$, so the sum is $3.5$ and the QMC estimate is $\widehat\theta_{\bullet}^{(7)}=3.5/7=0.5000$, exact to
the displayed precision. The symmetry of the Sobol' net about $\tfrac12$ has reproduced the symmetry of the
integrand and hit the truth on the nose.

**Part B: an asymmetric case ($\mu=0.5$).** Now the integrand is no longer symmetric and the integral
$\theta_{\bullet}=\int\mathrm{expit}(0.5+x)\phi(x)\,dx$ has no closed form (@thm-logit-no-closed-form); a
high-accuracy reference value is $\theta_{\bullet}=0.6020$, obtained by a high-order Gauss-Hermite rule (the
Gaussian-weight analogue of the Gauss-Legendre quadrature of @thm-quadrature-error), which for this smooth
one-dimensional integrand returns far more correct digits than we display and serves as ground truth against
which to measure the seven-point QMC estimate. The seven node values shift to

| $k$ | $x=\Phi^{-1}(k/8)$ | $\mathrm{expit}(0.5+x)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $-1.1503$ | $0.3429$ |
| 2 | $-0.6745$ | $0.4565$ |
| 3 | $-0.3186$ | $0.5452$ |
| 4 | $0$ | $0.6225$ |
| 5 | $0.3186$ | $0.6939$ |
| 6 | $0.6745$ | $0.7640$ |
| 7 | $1.1503$ | $0.8389$ |

summing to $4.2639$, so $\widehat\theta_{\bullet}^{(7)}=4.2639/7=0.6091$, an error of $+0.0071$ against the
truth $0.6020$. Refining the Sobol' net by taking the first $N$ van der Corput points for $N=4,8,16,\dots$
gives a deterministic, monotone approach to the truth:

| $N$ | $\widehat\theta_{\bullet}^{(N)}$ | error | $\big|\widehat\theta_{\bullet}^{(N)}-\widehat\theta_{\bullet}^{(N/2)}\big|$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | $0.5465$ | $-0.0556$ | |
| 8 | $0.5658$ | $-0.0363$ | $0.0193$ |
| 16 | $0.5809$ | $-0.0212$ | $0.0151$ |
| 32 | $0.5903$ | $-0.0117$ | $0.0095$ |
| 64 | $0.5958$ | $-0.0062$ | $0.0054$ |
| 128 | $0.5987$ | $-0.0033$ | $0.0030$ |

The error roughly halves at each doubling of $N$, consistent with the $O((\log N)/N)$ ceiling of
@thm-hypercube-integration in $d=1$, and the last column, the $N$-versus-$N/2$ gap, is the practical
convergence diagnostic of @def-integration-error-monitoring: it shrinks below $0.005$ by $N=128$, signaling
that the integration error is now small relative to typical posterior uncertainty.

**Contrast with plain Monte Carlo.** Estimating the same $\theta_{\bullet}=0.6020$ with $N=64$ independent
uniform draws in place of the Sobol' net gives, across five seeds, the estimates
$0.5938,\ 0.6173,\ 0.6095,\ 0.6073,\ 0.6613$, with errors ranging from $-0.008$ to $+0.059$; the spread is
consistent with the root-mean-square error ceiling $\sigma/\sqrt{64}\le 1/(2\cdot 8)=0.0625$ of
@thm-mc-rmse and its bounded-integrand refinement. At the same cost the deterministic QMC estimate
$0.5958$ has error $-0.0062$, and, unlike the Monte Carlo estimates, it is reproducible and a smooth
function of $\mu$, the two properties that matter inside a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo fit. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The single covariate hid the copula. The next example traces one Sobol' point through the full
two-covariate pipeline so that the Cholesky and normal-transform steps of @eq-qmc-pipeline are visible.

::: {#exm-qmc-copula-trace}
## A two-covariate pipeline trace
Let study $j$ have two covariates with standard normal margins $X_1,X_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and
Gaussian-copula correlation $\rho=0.5$, so
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with Cholesky factor
$L=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0.5&\sqrt{0.75}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0.5&0.8660\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Take the Sobol' point $\mathbf{u}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac14)$ and push it through @eq-qmc-pipeline:
$$
\mathbf{z}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf{u})=\big(\Phi^{-1}(0.5),\Phi^{-1}(0.25)\big)=(0,\,-0.6745);
$$
$$
\tilde{\mathbf{z}}=L\mathbf{z}=\big(1\cdot 0,\;0.5\cdot 0+0.8660\cdot(-0.6745)\big)=(0,\,-0.5841);
$$
$$
\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\Phi(\tilde{\mathbf{z}})=\big(\Phi(0),\Phi(-0.5841)\big)=(0.5000,\,0.2796);
$$
$$
\mathbf{x}=\big(F_{j,1}^{-1}(0.5000),F_{j,2}^{-1}(0.2796)\big)=\big(\Phi^{-1}(0.5),\Phi^{-1}(0.2796)\big)=(0,\,-0.5841),
$$
the last step using that the margins are standard normal, so $F_{j,i}^{-1}=\Phi^{-1}$ and
$\mathbf{x}=\tilde{\mathbf{z}}$. The correlation has done its work: the second coordinate has been shrunk
from its uncorrelated value $-0.6745$ toward the first coordinate's value $0$, the imprint of the positive
dependence $\rho=0.5$. If the arm has linear predictor $\eta(\mathbf{x})=x_1+0.5\,x_2$ on the logit scale,
this node contributes $\mathrm{expit}(0+0.5\cdot(-0.5841))=\mathrm{expit}(-0.2921)=0.4275$ to the average
@eq-qmc-fixed-nodes.

To watch the dependence act across several nodes at once, the table below runs the four quarter-points
$\mathbf{u}\in\{(\tfrac14,\tfrac14),(\tfrac14,\tfrac34),(\tfrac34,\tfrac14),(\tfrac34,\tfrac34)\}$ through the
same pipeline (standard normal margins, so $\mathbf{x}=\tilde{\mathbf{z}}$), showing side by side the
uncorrelated second coordinate $z_2=\Phi^{-1}(u_2)$ and the correlated value $x_2=\tilde z_2$ that the
Cholesky step produces, together with the node's contribution under $\eta(\mathbf{x})=x_1+0.5\,x_2$:

| $\mathbf{u}$ | $\mathbf{z}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathbf{u})$ | $z_2$ before | $x_2$ after | $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ | $\mathrm{expit}(x_1+0.5x_2)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$ | $(-0.6745,-0.6745)$ | $-0.6745$ | $-0.9214$ | $(-0.6745,-0.9214)$ | $0.2432$ |
| $(\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$ | $(-0.6745,\;0.6745)$ | $0.6745$ | $0.2469$ | $(-0.6745,\;0.2469)$ | $0.3656$ |
| $(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)$ | $(\;0.6745,-0.6745)$ | $-0.6745$ | $-0.2469$ | $(\;0.6745,-0.2469)$ | $0.6344$ |
| $(\tfrac34,\tfrac34)$ | $(\;0.6745,\;0.6745)$ | $0.6745$ | $0.9214$ | $(\;0.6745,\;0.9214)$ | $0.7568$ |

Reading the two middle columns exhibits the copula at work. When the two normal scores agree in sign (first
and last rows) the positive correlation pushes $x_2$ further out, from $\mp0.6745$ to $\mp0.9214$; when they
disagree (middle two rows) it pulls $x_2$ in toward zero, from $\pm0.6745$ to $\pm0.2469$. The margins are
untouched throughout, only the pairing of the coordinates changes, which is exactly what a copula does. The
four contributions average to $0.5000$ here only because this symmetric net mirrors the symmetric integrand,
as in Part A of @exm-qmc-logit; the lesson of the table is the visible shrinkage in the $x_2$ column, not
the average. Repeating over a full Sobol' net and averaging gives $\theta_{\bullet jk}$ exactly as in
@exm-qmc-logit, now with the covariate dependence correctly imposed by the single Cholesky factor $L$;
@exr-qmc-logit-pipeline asks you to carry this out for a different linear predictor and to compare the
result against the independent ($\rho=0$) case. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-qmc-notes}

The numerical-integration program of this chapter is the computational core of multilevel network
meta-regression as developed by @phillippo2020mlnmr and @phillippo2019thesis, whose Chapter 5 lays out the
Sobol'-plus-copula pipeline of @thm-hypercube-integration and is implemented in the `multinma` package; the
unanchored extension of Chapter 26 (@chandler2025mlumr) reuses the same machinery. The general principle
that the aggregate likelihood is an integral of the response-scale conditional mean, and therefore demands
numerical integration whenever the link is nonlinear, is the subject of Chapter 20 (@thm-aggregation,
@thm-aggregation-bias, @thm-logit-no-closed-form); the discrete-outcome aggregate likelihoods of Chapter 21
rest on the same integral through the success probabilities.

The classical numerical analysis is standard. Gauss-Legendre quadrature and the error formula
@eq-qmc-gauss-error, with its derivation through Hermite interpolation and the Legendre normalization
$\int_{-1}^{1}P_k^2=2/(2k+1)$, are in Stoer and Bulirsch, *Introduction to Numerical Analysis* (Section
3.6); the orthogonality of Legendre polynomials and the Hermite remainder formula are the two classical
facts the proof invokes. The dimension-free Monte Carlo rate @thm-mc-rmse is the variance of a sample mean
together with the central limit theorem of Chapter 5; the bounded-integrand variance ceiling is Popoviciu's
inequality. The Koksma-Hlawka inequality @thm-koksma-hlawka is due to Koksma (1942/43) in one dimension and
Hlawka (1961) in several; the one-dimensional identity @eq-qmc-koksma-identity and its proof by the
fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini are elementary and self-contained here, and the multidimensional
Hardy-Krause identity, the definitions of Vitali and Hardy-Krause variation, and the low-discrepancy rate
$D_N^{*}=O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ are developed in Niederreiter, *Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo
Methods* (1992, Chapters 2 and 4). Sobol' sequences and their digital-net structure are from @sobol1967;
the direction numbers used in modern software are those of Joe and Kuo (2008); randomized (scrambled) nets,
which recover near-optimal rates for integrands of unbounded variation, are due to Owen (1998). The
copula apparatus is Sklar's theorem @thm-sklar (@sklar1959), with the textbook development in Nelsen, *An
Introduction to Copulas* (2006); the Gaussian copula and its zero tail dependence are standard, and the
bivariate normal probabilities needed to evaluate (though not to sample) the Gaussian copula are Owen's
tabulated integral (@owen1956). The probability integral transform @thm-inverse-cdf and the quantile
coupling inequality @lem-quantile-galois are elementary measure theory.

The forward connections are to the rest of Part V. The fixed-node likelihood @eq-qmc-fixed-nodes is what
makes the aggregate model differentiable in the parameters and hence amenable to the Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo of Chapter 24 (@def-hmc, @carpenter2017stan, @def-centered-noncentered), where the integration error
@eq-qmc-pipeline-error is monitored alongside the Markov chain Monte Carlo error
(@def-integration-error-monitoring, @def-mcmc-ess). The same pipeline computes the target-population
estimand integral of Chapter 23 (@thm-target-population-integral), which is the device by which ML-NMR
transports a relative effect to a population represented by neither trial, and underwrites the
identifiability and generalization results @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study and @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma.

This chapter corresponds to results H.12 (Gauss-Legendre quadrature error), H.13 (Monte Carlo
root-mean-square error), H.14 (Koksma-Hlawka), H.15 (Sobol' nets), H.16 (Sklar's theorem), H.17 (the
Gaussian copula), H.18 (the inverse-CDF transform), and H.19 (the unit-hypercube integration pipeline) of
the proof catalogue in `proofs/H_ml_nmr.md`, together with the integration-error material of
`proofs/I_computation.md` (I.4), which Chapter 24 develops. The Coq development in `ITC_Coq/theories/`
formalizes the population-adjustment and causal core of the book but not the numerical-integration theory;
the results of this chapter are pen-and-paper, and no machine-checked tags are claimed.

## Exercises {#sec-qmc-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are
low-barrier warm-ups that need no new proof technique; the later ones build in mathematical demand.

::: {#exr-qmc-diagnostic-read}
**(Warm-up: reading the convergence diagnostic.)** Look at the refinement table in Part B of
@exm-qmc-logit, whose last column is the $N$-versus-$N/2$ gap. At which $N$ does that gap first fall below
$0.005$? Using the practical guidance of @sec-qmc-pipeline, state in one sentence what a researcher should
conclude about whether $N$ is large enough, and name one situation in which you would insist on a smaller
gap even though $0.005$ looks small.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-correlation-interp}
**(Interpretation: why dependence matters when margins do not change.)** An aggregate arm reports the same
marginal means and standard deviations for two effect modifiers, but you must choose their Gaussian-copula
correlation, either $\rho=0$ or $\rho=0.5$. Without computing anything, argue whether the aggregate event
probability $\theta_{\bullet}$ can differ between the two choices, and explain why, appealing to the fact
that the response probability is a nonlinear function of the linear predictor (contrast this with what would
happen under an identity link). Then state which single additional piece of information, if the study
reported it, would let you pin down the appropriate $\rho$, and relate your answer to the caution in
@sec-qmc-gaussian that a reported Pearson correlation is not in general the latent $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-gauss-two-node}
**Two-node Gauss-Legendre by hand.** Find the nodes and weights of the two-node Gauss-Legendre rule on
$[-1,1]$ by requiring exactness on $1,x,x^2,x^3$; you should obtain $x_{1,2}=\pm 1/\sqrt 3$,
$w_1=w_2=1$. Verify the degree-of-exactness claim of @thm-quadrature-error(1) by checking that the rule
integrates $x^3$ exactly but not $x^4$, and confirm the error constant @eq-qmc-gauss-error for $k=2$ by
evaluating both sides on $f(x)=x^4$.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-mc-variance}
**Monte Carlo sample size.** Using the bounded-integrand variance ceiling of @thm-mc-rmse, find the
smallest number of independent draws $N$ guaranteeing a Monte Carlo root-mean-square error below $0.001$
for a logit aggregate probability, and compare with the number of Sobol' points needed for the same error
under the $O((\log N)/N)$ rate of @thm-hypercube-integration in one dimension (take the implied constant to
be $1$). Comment on the gap and on why it widens as the target accuracy tightens.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-discrepancy}
**Discrepancy of a grid versus a sequence.** Compute the star discrepancy (@def-star-discrepancy) of the
equally spaced left-endpoint grid $\{0,\tfrac1N,\dots,\tfrac{N-1}{N}\}$ in one dimension, and of the
midpoint grid $\{\tfrac{1}{2N},\tfrac{3}{2N},\dots,\tfrac{2N-1}{2N}\}$. Show that both are $O(1/N)$, and
explain why a low-discrepancy *sequence* such as van der Corput is nonetheless preferred in practice over a
grid, even though both attain the $1/N$ rate. (Hint: consider what happens to a grid when $N$ is increased
by one, versus appending one point to a sequence.)
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-pit-discrete}
**The transform on a discrete margin.** Let $X$ be Bernoulli with $P(X=1)=0.3$, with distribution function
$F$. Verify directly that @thm-inverse-cdf(1) holds, that is $F^{-1}(U)\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.3)$ for
$U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, by computing $F^{-1}(u)$ for $u\in(0,1)$. Then show that $F(X)$ takes only two
values and is not uniform, confirming the failure of @thm-inverse-cdf(2) for discrete margins. Explain in
one sentence how this produces a jump in the pipeline integrand $\psi$ of @thm-hypercube-integration, and
why the jump threatens the Koksma-Hlawka rate once the copula correlates this covariate with another.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-gaussian-copula-cov}
**($\star$) Gaussian copula correlation versus covariate correlation.** Two covariates have standard normal
margins and a Gaussian copula with latent correlation $\rho$. Show that their Pearson correlation as
covariates equals $\rho$ exactly. Then replace the first margin by an exponential distribution (still with
a Gaussian copula at latent correlation $\rho$) and argue, without a full computation, that the covariate
Pearson correlation is now strictly smaller in magnitude than $\rho$, while the Spearman rank correlation
is unchanged. Relate your finding to the remark in @sec-qmc-gaussian that $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is the
correlation of the latent normals, not of the covariates.
:::

::: {#exr-qmc-logit-pipeline}
**($\star$) A QMC logit integral with two correlated covariates.** Extend @exm-qmc-logit to two covariates with
standard normal margins, Gaussian-copula correlation $\rho=0.5$, and linear predictor
$\eta(\mathbf{x})=0.5+x_1+0.5\,x_2$ on the logit scale. Using the four two-dimensional Sobol' points
$\mathbf{u}\in\{(\tfrac12,\tfrac12),(\tfrac14,\tfrac34),(\tfrac34,\tfrac14),(\tfrac18,\tfrac58)\}$, run the
pipeline @eq-qmc-pipeline on each (you computed one such trace in @exm-qmc-copula-trace), evaluate
$\mathrm{expit}(\eta(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}))$, and report the four-point QMC estimate of $\theta_{\bullet}$.
Then set $\rho=0$ and recompute, and explain why the estimate changes even though the margins are
unchanged, connecting your answer to the aggregation-bias and ecological-bias discussion of Chapter 20
(@thm-aggregation-bias, @def-ecological-bias).
:::
